26967.e: In the past herdsmen used the alphorn to send each other signals over long distances. You could hear it far across the mountains.
26967.m: Herdsmen sent each other signals with the alphorn.

26968.q: What does an alphorn not have?
26968.e: The alphorn has no finger holes, keys or valves. The notes come only from the player’s lips.
26968.m: An alphorn has no finger holes and keys.

26969.q: Where does the bottom end of the alphorn rest while you play?
26969.e: Because the alphorn is so long, the curved end stands on the ground while you play. The player stands upright behind it.
26969.m: While you play, the alphorn rests on the ground.

26970.q: Which music do you often hear together with the alphorn at folk festivals?
26970.e: At Swiss folk festivals alphorn players and yodellers often perform together. Both are part of folk music.
26970.m: Alphorn and yodelling are part of Swiss folk music.

26971.q: Where does the Unspunnen Festival take place?
26971.e: The Unspunnen Festival takes place in Interlaken in the Bernese Oberland. It is named after the ruined Unspunnen Castle.
26971.m: The Unspunnen Festival is in Interlaken.

26972.q: What is thrown as far as possible at the Unspunnen Festival?
26972.e: In stone throwing, strong men throw the Unspunnen Stone as far as they can. It is the best-known contest at the festival.
26972.m: At the Unspunnen Festival people throw a heavy stone.

26973.q: Roughly how heavy is the Unspunnen Stone?
26973.e: The Unspunnen Stone originally weighed 83.5 kilograms. Only very strong men can throw it far.
26973.m: The Unspunnen Stone weighs about 83 kilograms.

26974.q: In which year did the first Unspunnen Festival take place?
26974.e: The first Unspunnen Festival took place in 1805. It was meant to bring town and country closer together again.
26974.m: The first Unspunnen Festival took place in 1805.

26975.q: What do many visitors and performers wear at the Unspunnen Festival?
26975.e: At the Unspunnen Festival costume groups from all over Switzerland show their beautiful traditional costumes. It is also a big costume festival.
26975.m: At the Unspunnen Festival people wear beautiful traditional costumes.

26976.q: Roughly how often does the Unspunnen Festival take place today?
26976.e: The Unspunnen Festival does not take place every year. Today it is held about every twelve years, most recently in 2017.
26976.m: The Unspunnen Festival takes place about every twelve years.

26977.q: What has happened to the Unspunnen Stone more than once?
26977.e: The Unspunnen Stone got stolen in 1984 and 2005. After the first theft it came back in 2001; since 2005 it has been missing, so today people throw a copy.
26977.m: The Unspunnen Stone has been stolen twice.

26978.q: In which city does the Zibelemärit take place?
26978.e: The Zibelemärit is a famous market in the city of Bern. It takes place on squares and in lanes of the old town.
26978.m: The Zibelemärit takes place in Bern.

26979.q: What is mainly sold at the Zibelemärit?
26979.e: “Zibele” is the Bernese German word for onions. At the market there are tonnes of onions.
26979.m: At the Zibelemärit you buy onions.

26980.q: In which month does the Zibelemärit take place?
26980.e: The Zibelemärit takes place every year at the end of November. By then it is often already cold in Bern.

26981.q: How are the onions at the Zibelemärit often artistically presented?
26981.e: Farmers plait the onions into long strings and wreaths. These onion plaits are very popular.
26981.m: At the Zibelemärit there are plaited strings of onions.

26982.q: What do children like to throw at each other at the Zibelemärit?
26982.e: At the Zibelemärit children and teenagers throw confetti. Some also tap people with little plastic hammers.
26982.m: Lots of confetti flies at the Zibelemärit.

26983.q: Which baked dish with onions do people eat at the Zibelemärit?
26983.e: At the Zibelemärit many stalls sell warm onion tart. It is as much a part of the market as the onion plaits.
26983.m: At the Zibelemärit people eat onion tart.

26984.q: On which day of the week does the Zibelemärit take place?
26984.e: The Zibelemärit is always on the fourth Monday in November. Many people in Bern take the day off for it.
26984.m: The Zibelemärit is on a Monday.

26985.q: Which geological eon makes up by far the largest part of Earth's history?
26985.e: The Precambrian lasted from the formation of the Earth until around 540 million years ago. That is almost nine tenths of all of Earth's history.
26985.m: The Precambrian is the longest section of Earth's history.

26987.q: Which period of the Palaeozoic is named after a county in England?
26987.e: The Devonian is named after the county of Devon in south-west England. Rocks from this time were studied there early on.
26987.m: The Devonian is named after an English county.

26988.q: Which mountain range is the Jurassic period named after?
26988.e: The name comes from the Jura mountains in Switzerland and France. Many limestone rocks from this time are found there.
26988.m: The Jurassic period is named after a Swiss mountain range.

26989.q: Which geological era do we live in today?
26989.e: The Cenozoic began around 66 million years ago, after the dinosaurs died out. It continues to this day.
26989.m: We live in the Cenozoic era.

26990.q: What is the end of the Permian, around 252 million years ago, known for?
26990.e: At the end of the Permian, most species of sea animals died out. It was the worst mass extinction in Earth's history.
26990.m: The biggest mass extinction happened at the end of the Permian.

26991.q: Where is the crater of the asteroid that helped wipe out the dinosaurs around 66 million years ago?
26991.e: The Chicxulub crater is on the Yucatán peninsula in Mexico. The impact ended the Cretaceous period.
26991.m: The impact crater from the end of the Cretaceous is in Mexico.

26992.q: What is the Carboniferous period named after?
26992.e: “Carbo” is Latin for coal. Many coal deposits formed from huge swamp forests of this time.
26992.m: The Carboniferous is named after coal.

26993.q: What is meant by the Cambrian explosion?
a: The rapid appearance of many animal groups
The impact of a giant meteorite
26993.e: At the start of the Cambrian, almost all of today's animal phyla appeared in a short time, geologically speaking. “Explosion” refers to this rapid variety.
26993.m: In the Cambrian explosion, many new animal groups appeared quickly.

26994.q: About how many years ago did the Cambrian begin?
26994.e: The Cambrian began around 540 million years ago. It marks the start of the Palaeozoic era.
26994.m: The Cambrian began around 540 million years ago.

26995.q: Where did the animals of the Cambrian explosion live?
26995.e: In the Cambrian there was no animal life on land yet. All the animals of this time lived in water.
26995.m: The animals of the Cambrian all lived in the sea.

26996.q: How do we know which animals lived in the Cambrian?
a: From stories told by the first humans
26996.e: There were no humans in the Cambrian. Fossilised remains in rock tell us what the animals looked like.
26996.m: Fossils show which animals lived in the Cambrian.

26997.q: Why are the fossils from the Burgess Shale especially valuable?
a: Soft body parts were preserved too
They are all made of pure gold
26997.e: Normally only hard parts such as shells become fossils. In the Burgess Shale, soft parts were preserved too, for example from worms.
26997.m: Even soft animals are fossilised in the Burgess Shale.

26998.q: How many eyes did the Cambrian animal Opabinia have?
26998.e: Opabinia had five eyes on stalks and a long trunk with a grabbing claw. It was found in the Burgess Shale.

26999.q: What role did Anomalocaris play in the Cambrian sea?
a: It was a plant-eater on land
26999.e: Anomalocaris was one of the largest animals of its time. It caught prey with grasping limbs on its head.
26999.m: Anomalocaris was a predator in the Cambrian sea.

27000.e: The Cambrian began around 540 million years ago. The name comes from Cambria, the old name for Wales.
27000.m: The Cambrian is a period of Earth's history.

27002.q: Where does the trilobite get its name from?
a: Its body is divided into three lengthwise parts
It had three pairs of legs
27002.e: “Trilobite” means “three-lobed”. Along its length, the shell has a middle part and two side parts.
27002.m: The trilobite is named after its three lengthwise lobes.

27003.q: Did trilobites live at the same time as the dinosaurs?
a: No, they had already died out
Yes, at exactly the same time
No, they only appeared after the dinosaurs
Yes, and they still live today
27003.e: The last trilobites died out around 250 million years ago in a great mass extinction. The first dinosaurs only appeared after that.
27003.m: Trilobites died out before the dinosaurs.

27004.q: What were the lenses in trilobites' eyes made of?
27004.e: The eye lenses of trilobites were made of the mineral calcite. That is why their eyes are often well fossilised.
27004.m: Trilobites saw through lenses made of calcite.

27005.q: How did many trilobites protect themselves when in danger?
27005.e: Many trilobites could roll up like a woodlouse. That way the hard back shell protected the soft underside.
27005.m: Trilobites rolled up when in danger.

27006.q: Why are several shells sometimes found from a single trilobite?
27006.e: Like crabs, trilobites had to shed their stiff shell in order to grow. The empty shells could also become fossils.
27006.m: Trilobites moulted in order to grow.

27007.q: What do geologists often use trilobites for?
a: As index fossils for the Palaeozoic
As a raw material for petrol
As clocks for low and high tide
27007.e: Trilobites changed quickly and were widespread. That is why they can be used to date rock layers from the Palaeozoic.
27007.m: Trilobites help to date old rock layers.

27008.q: Which animal group did ammonites belong to?
27008.e: Ammonites were cephalopods, like today's octopuses and squid. They lived in a shell with chambers.

27009.q: Where does the ammonite get its name from?
27009.e: The god Amun was shown with ram's horns. The coiled shells reminded people of these horns, which is why they were also called horns of Ammon.
27009.m: Ammonites remind people of the ram's horns of the god Amun.

27010.q: What were the chambers in an ammonite's shell for?
27010.e: The animal only lived in the front chamber. The back chambers held gas and liquid, which let it control how it floated.
27010.m: The chambers helped the ammonite float.

27011.q: When did the ammonites die out?
a: At the end of the Cretaceous
At the end of the Cambrian
27011.e: The ammonites disappeared around 66 million years ago. They died out at the same time as the dinosaurs that were not birds.
27011.m: The ammonites died out together with the dinosaurs.

27012.q: Which animal alive today has a chambered shell similar to the ammonites?
27012.e: The nautilus is a cephalopod with a chambered limestone shell. It lives in the Pacific and Indian Oceans.
27012.m: The nautilus has a chambered shell like an ammonite.

27013.q: In which part of its shell did the ammonite live?
27013.e: The animal sat in the large front chamber. The back chambers were filled with gas and liquid and connected by a thin tube.
27013.m: The ammonite lived in the front chamber.

27014.q: Why are ammonites good index fossils?
a: Their species changed quickly and were widespread
They only lived in one single place
They are all the same size
27014.e: Each ammonite species only lived for a short time but was found in many seas. That way, layers of the same age far apart can be recognised.
27014.m: Ammonites show the age of rock layers.

27015.q: What do you call the fossilised remains of living things such as ammonites?
27015.e: Fossils are remains or traces of living things that were preserved in rock a very long time ago. Ammonites are among the most common fossils.

27016.q: Which condition especially helps an animal to become a fossil?
a: It is quickly covered by mud
It lies in the sun for a long time
It lies on a mountain top
27016.e: If a body is quickly covered by sand or mud, there is no oxygen and decay slows down. Minerals can then gradually replace the remains.
27016.m: Being covered quickly by mud helps fossilisation.

27017.e: Coprolites are fossilised droppings. They show what an animal ate.
27017.m: Fossilised poo is called a coprolite.

a: A cast of the inside of a shell
A stone from a fossilised fruit
The innermost part of the Earth
27018.e: Sediment fills an empty shell. If the shell later dissolves, the filling remains as a copy of the inside.
27018.m: An internal mould shows the inside shape of a shell.

27019.q: What kind of fossil are fossilised footprints?
27019.e: Trace fossils do not show the animal itself but what it did. They include trackways, burrows and bite marks.

27020.q: Which body parts most often become fossils?
a: Hard parts such as bones and shells
Soft parts such as skin and muscles
27020.e: Soft tissue usually breaks down quickly. Hard parts such as teeth, bones and shells last longer and can become fossils.
27020.m: Mainly hard body parts become fossils.

27021.q: How have whole mammoths with skin and hair been preserved to this day?
a: They dried out in the desert
27021.e: Mammoths have been found in the permafrost of Siberia and Alaska. The cold stopped the bodies from rotting.
27021.m: Mammoths were preserved deep-frozen in permafrost.

27022.e: Amber formed from the resin of prehistoric trees. Over millions of years the resin became hard.

27023.q: Why are insects in amber so well preserved?
a: The resin sealed them in airtight
They were dried in the sun
27023.e: Insects got stuck in the sticky resin and were completely surrounded. Without air they could not rot. Experts call such trapped objects inclusions.
27023.m: Insects in amber are sealed in airtight.

27024.q: Which living things are found most often in amber?
27024.e: Small insects such as midges, flies and ants easily got stuck in the sticky resin. Bigger animals could usually free themselves.

27025.q: What was the famous Amber Room?
a: A splendid room with walls made of amber
27025.e: The Amber Room was a room whose walls were covered with panels of amber. It vanished without trace in the Second World War.
27025.m: The Amber Room was a room with walls made of amber.

27026.q: Why is amber often washed up on Baltic Sea beaches during storms?
a: It is hardly heavier than water
27026.e: Amber is only a little denser than water. So the waves can easily move it and wash it onto the beach; in very salty water it even floats.
27026.m: Amber is so light that waves wash it onto the beach.

27028.q: Which word comes from the Greek name for amber?
27028.e: In Greek, amber is called “elektron”. If you rub it, it attracts tiny particles, and this gave rise to the word electricity.
27028.m: Electricity is named after the Greek word for amber.

27029.q: What was found in a piece of amber from Myanmar in 2016?
a: Part of a feathered dinosaur tail
27029.e: In the amber, about 99 million years old, there was a small tail with feathers. It came from a young meat-eating dinosaur.
27029.m: A dinosaur's feathered tail was found in amber.

27030.q: What is especially striking about the prehistoric reptile Tanystropheus from Monte San Giorgio?
27030.e: Tanystropheus's neck was longer than its body and tail together. It probably hunted fish and squid in coastal waters.
27030.m: Tanystropheus had an extremely long neck.

27031.q: Why is Monte San Giorgio a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site?
27031.e: The mountain has been a World Heritage Site since 2003. It is one of the best sites for marine fossils from the Triassic.
27031.m: Monte San Giorgio is a World Natural Heritage Site because of its fossils.

27032.q: Which period do the famous marine fossils of Monte San Giorgio come from?
27032.e: The fossils are around 245 to 230 million years old. That matches the Middle Triassic.
27032.m: The fossils of Monte San Giorgio come from the Triassic.

27034.q: What was made from the oil shale of Monte San Giorgio from 1908 onwards?
27034.e: At the Spinirolo works, the oily rock was turned into an ointment for the skin called Saurol. Mining ended around 1960.
27034.m: A skin ointment was made from the oil shale of Monte San Giorgio.

27035.q: What is special about the fossil Ticinosuchus from Monte San Giorgio?
27035.e: Ticinosuchus lived on land around 240 million years ago and was washed into the sea. Its name means “Ticino crocodile”.
27035.m: Ticinosuchus was a land reptile from Ticino.

27036.q: Which architect from Ticino redesigned the fossil museum in Meride?
27036.e: Mario Botta redesigned and extended the museum. It reopened on 13 October 2012.
27036.m: Mario Botta redesigned the fossil museum in Meride.

27037.q: What are the researchers called who dig up and study fossils, as on Monte San Giorgio?
27037.e: Palaeontologists study prehistoric living things from their fossils. They have been digging on Monte San Giorgio for over 100 years.

27038.q: How high is Monte San Giorgio?
27038.e: The summit is 1,097 metres above sea level. It rises between two arms of Lake Lugano.
27038.m: Monte San Giorgio is around 1,100 metres high.

27039.q: In which canton is Frick, where many Plateosaurus were found?
27039.e: Frick is in the Fricktal valley in the canton of Aargau. Many dinosaur bones came to light there in a clay pit.
27039.m: Frick, with its Plateosaurus, is in Aargau.

27040.e: Plateosaurus was a plant-eater. With its long neck it could reach leaves high up.

27041.q: Which time does the Plateosaurus from Frick come from?
27041.e: Plateosaurus lived in the Late Triassic around 210 million years ago. It is one of the early large dinosaurs.
27041.m: Plateosaurus lived in the late Triassic.

27042.q: According to what we know today, how did Plateosaurus move around?
27042.e: Its front legs were shorter than its back legs and were used for grasping. So Plateosaurus walked on two legs.

27043.q: Where in Frick were the Plateosaurus bones found?
a: In the bed of the Rhine
27043.e: In the Frick clay pit, clay is dug for bricks and roof tiles. Many dinosaur bones came to light during digging.
27043.m: The Plateosaurus of Frick lay in a clay pit.

27044.q: How long could a Plateosaurus grow?
27044.e: Large Plateosaurus grew up to ten metres long. That made them some of the first large dinosaurs.
27044.m: Plateosaurus grew up to about ten metres long.

27045.q: What does the Dinosaur Museum in Frick mainly show?
a: Dinosaur finds from the Frick clay pit
Minerals from all over the world
27045.e: The museum opened in 1991. Its showpiece is an almost complete Plateosaurus skeleton.
27045.m: In the Dinosaur Museum in Frick you can see dinosaurs from Aargau.

27046.q: What did the meat-eating dinosaurs whose bones were found in Frick eat?
27046.e: A meat-eating dinosaur was also found in Frick. Remains of its last prey were still in its stomach.
27046.m: Meat-eating dinosaurs also lived in Frick.

27047.q: Which animals already lived in Frick at the time of Plateosaurus and still exist today?
27047.e: Remains of the early turtle Proganochelys were found in Frick. It is over 200 million years old and is thought to be the oldest turtle in Switzerland.
27047.m: Turtles already existed at the time of the first dinosaurs.

27048.e: Archaeopteryx had feathers and wings like a bird. It is thought to be one of the oldest known birds.
27048.m: Archaeopteryx is called the first bird.

27049.q: In which country were the fossils of Archaeopteryx found?
27049.e: All Archaeopteryx finds come from Bavaria in Germany. They lay in the fine layered limestone of the area around Solnhofen.

27050.q: Which period does Archaeopteryx come from?
27050.e: Archaeopteryx lived around 150 million years ago in the late Jurassic. At that time there were lagoons of a warm sea near Solnhofen.

27051.q: Which feature did Archaeopteryx have that today's birds do not?
27051.e: Archaeopteryx had teeth, claws on its wings and a long bony tail. Today's birds have no teeth.
27051.m: Unlike today's birds, Archaeopteryx had teeth.

27052.q: Why is Archaeopteryx so important for research?
a: It combines features of reptiles and birds
It was the biggest bird of all time
27052.e: Archaeopteryx had feathers like a bird and teeth and a tail like a reptile. It is seen as a link between dinosaurs and birds.
27052.m: Archaeopteryx is a link between dinosaurs and birds.

27053.q: What does the name Archaeopteryx mean?
27053.e: The name comes from Greek: “archaios” means ancient and “pteryx” means wing.

27054.q: What was described in 1861 as the first clue to Archaeopteryx?
27054.e: In 1861 Hermann von Meyer described a single feather from the Solnhofen limestone. Shortly afterwards a skeleton was found too.
27054.m: The first Archaeopteryx find was a single feather.

27055.e: In Pangaea, almost all of the Earth's land was joined into one single continent.

27056.q: What does the name Pangaea mean?
27056.e: The name comes from Greek: “pan” means whole or all and “gaia” means Earth.

27057.e: Pangaea formed towards the end of the Palaeozoic. In the Jurassic, around 200 million years ago, it began to break up.
27057.m: Pangaea existed around 300 to 200 million years ago.

27058.e: Pangaea was surrounded by a huge world ocean called Panthalassa. That means “whole sea”.
27058.m: Pangaea lay in a giant ocean.

27059.q: Which two big parts did Pangaea first break into?
27059.e: Pangaea split into the northern continent Laurasia and the southern continent Gondwana. These later broke up further.
27059.m: Pangaea broke up into Laurasia and Gondwana.

27060.q: What is found in many rocks of the Alps as proof that there was once a sea there?
27060.e: Many Alpine rocks formed from deposits on the floor of the ancient Tethys Sea. Mussels and other sea creatures are fossilised in them.
27060.m: Fossilised sea creatures show that the Alps were once sea floor.

27061.q: Which animals lived at the time when Pangaea was still joined together?
27061.e: The first dinosaurs appeared in the Triassic. At that time the continents still formed Pangaea.
27061.m: The first dinosaurs lived on the supercontinent Pangaea.

27062.q: Why are fossils of the same Triassic land animals found on continents that are now far apart?
a: The continents were joined back then
The animals swam across the oceans
The animals flew between the continents
27062.e: At the time of Pangaea, the land masses were connected. Land animals could spread across the whole supercontinent.
27062.m: Because the continents were connected, the same animals lived far apart.

27063.q: Who set out the theory of continental drift in detail in 1915?
27063.e: Alfred Wegener published the book “The Origin of Continents and Oceans” in 1915. Many scientists rejected his idea at first.
27063.m: Alfred Wegener developed the theory of continental drift.

27064.e: Wegener was a meteorologist and studied the weather. He died in 1930 on an expedition in Greenland.
27064.m: Alfred Wegener was a meteorologist and polar explorer.

27065.q: Which observation gave Wegener his idea?
a: The coasts of Africa and South America fit together
The Alps get smaller every year
The Moon is moving away from the Earth
27065.e: The east coast of South America and the west coast of Africa fit together like jigsaw pieces. Wegener concluded that they were once joined.
27065.m: The coasts of Africa and South America fit like a jigsaw.

27066.q: Which reptile has been found as a fossil in both South America and Africa?
27066.e: Mesosaurus lived in fresh water and could not cross an ocean. Its fossils on both continents support the idea of continental drift.
27066.m: Mesosaurus fossils show that Africa and South America were joined.

27067.q: By about how much does the Atlantic grow each year?
a: By around 2 to 3 millimetres per century
27067.e: The plates are moving apart at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. That is about as fast as fingernails grow.
27067.m: The Atlantic gets a few centimetres wider every year.

27068.q: What is today's theory that explains the movement of the continents called?
27068.e: Since the 1960s, plate tectonics has explained how the Earth's crust moves in plates. It builds on Wegener's idea.

27069.q: Which tectonic plate collided with Asia and pushed up the Himalayas?
27069.e: India broke away from Gondwana and moved north. When it collided with Asia, the Himalayas piled up.
27069.m: The Himalayas formed when India collided with Asia.

27070.q: Which country lies right on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
27070.e: In Iceland, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge comes to the surface. That is why the island is slowly being pulled apart.
27070.m: Iceland lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

27071.q: In which canton are the dinosaur trackways of Vieux-Emosson?
27071.e: The trackways lie above the Emosson reservoir near the French border in the canton of Valais.
27071.m: The dinosaur trackways of Emosson are in Valais.

27072.q: How were the dinosaur trackways of Vieux-Emosson in Valais discovered?
a: A diver found them in the reservoir
27072.e: In late summer 1976, the old snow on the rock slabs melted. The tracks came to light by chance.
27072.m: The Emosson trackways appeared from under melting snow.

27073.q: At about what altitude are the Vieux-Emosson trackways?
27073.e: The tracks lie on sloping slabs of rock at around 2,400 metres above sea level. They are over 230 million years old.
27073.m: The Emosson trackways lie at around 2,400 metres.

27074.q: Why are dinosaur trackways found high up in the Alps today?
a: The rocks were lifted up when the Alps formed
The tracks were carried up by glaciers
27074.e: The tracks were once made in soft mud on coasts at sea level. When the Alps formed, these layers were lifted up and tilted.
27074.m: The formation of the Alps lifted old dinosaur tracks high up.

27075.q: In which Swiss protected area are there dinosaur trackways in the Val dal Diavel?
27075.e: Geologists discovered the trackways in the Val dal Diavel in 1961. The rock slab lies in the Swiss National Park in the Grisons.
27075.m: There are dinosaur trackways in the Swiss National Park.

27076.q: How many footprints were mapped on the rock slab in the National Park?
27076.e: On the slab, which is around 220 million years old, researchers counted more than 200 prints. They come from plant-eating prosauropods.
27076.m: Over 200 dinosaur footprints were found in the National Park.

27077.q: How can you look at the dinosaur trackways in the Swiss National Park today?
a: By cable car straight onto the slab
Only in the museum in Bern
27077.e: The rock slab is closed because of falling rocks. The larger prints can be seen with good binoculars from a mountain hut.
27077.m: You see the dinosaur tracks in the National Park with binoculars.

27078.q: What did an amateur researcher discover on a steep rock face on the Tinzenhorn in the Grisons?
27078.e: On the Tinzenhorn in Parc Ela he found tracks of sauropods. They are around 200 million years old and were tilted steeply when the Alps formed.
27078.m: There are dinosaur tracks on the Tinzenhorn.

27079.q: What shape were the big sauropod tracks on Piz Mitgel?
a: Long and narrow like snake tracks
27079.e: The prints are roundish and about 60 centimetres across. That is what the footprints of heavy, four-legged sauropods typically look like.
27079.m: Sauropod tracks on Piz Mitgel are large and roundish.

27080.q: In which country was the famous skeleton “Lucy” discovered in 1974?
27080.e: Lucy was found in November 1974 near Hadar in north-eastern Ethiopia. The area is rich in very old fossils.

27081.q: About how old is Lucy's skeleton?
27081.e: Volcanic ash near the find was dated using physical methods. It gave an age of about 3.2 million years.
27081.m: Lucy lived about 3.2 million years ago.

27082.q: Which song gave Lucy her nickname?
27082.e: On the evening after the find, this Beatles song was played again and again in the researchers' camp. That is how the skeleton got its name.
27082.m: Lucy is named after a Beatles song.

a: The skeleton of a female early human ancestor
27083.e: Lucy is a partial skeleton from Ethiopia, around 3.2 million years old. She belonged to an early species of human ancestor.
27083.m: Lucy is the skeleton of a female early human ancestor.

27084.q: About what share of Lucy's skeleton was found?
27084.e: About 40 per cent of Lucy's bones were found. For such an old fossil, that is an unusually large amount.
27084.m: About 40 per cent of Lucy's skeleton has survived.

27085.e: Lucy was only about 1.1 metres tall and weighed around 29 kilograms. That made her smaller than most ten-year-olds today.
27085.m: Lucy was about as tall as a young child.

27086.q: What does Lucy's skeleton show about how she moved?
a: She walked upright on two legs
She only walked on all fours
27086.e: Lucy's pelvis and legs show that she walked upright. At the same time, she could still climb well.
27086.m: Lucy already walked upright on two legs.

27087.q: On which continent did Lucy live?
27087.e: Lucy was found in Ethiopia in East Africa. Many of the oldest finds of human ancestors come from Africa.

27088.q: Where are Lucy's original bones kept today?
a: In the National Museum in Addis Ababa
In the British Museum in London
In the Natural History Museum in Basel
27088.e: The original is kept safe in the National Museum of Ethiopia in the capital. Visitors there usually see a cast.
27088.m: Lucy's bones are in the National Museum of Ethiopia.

27089.q: In which country is the Laetoli site with its famous footprints?
27089.e: Laetoli is in northern Tanzania in East Africa. Ancient footprints of human ancestors were found there.
27089.m: The Laetoli footprints are in Tanzania.

27090.q: About how old are the Laetoli footprints?
27090.e: The layers with the tracks have been dated to about 3.6 to 3.7 million years. So they are very old tracks of upright-walking human ancestors.
27090.m: The Laetoli footprints are almost four million years old.

27091.q: In what material were the Laetoli footprints preserved?
a: In the limestone of a cave
In the ice of a glacier
27091.e: A volcanic eruption covered the area with ash, which rain made damp and soft. After drying it became as hard as cement, and new ash covered the tracks.
27091.m: The Laetoli tracks were preserved in volcanic ash.

27092.q: In which year was the great Laetoli trackway fully dug out?
27092.e: Fossilised animal tracks were already found at Laetoli in 1976. The long trackway of the human ancestors was uncovered in 1978.
27092.m: The Laetoli trackway was dug out in the 1970s.

27093.q: About how long is the famous Laetoli trackway?
27093.e: The footprints stretch over a good 20 metres. Depending on the measurement, 24 to 27 metres is given.
27093.m: The Laetoli trackway is about as long as a swimming pool.

27094.q: According to the usual interpretation, how many individuals made the main Laetoli trackway?
27094.e: You can see two tracks side by side, and a third individual apparently stepped in the prints of another. That is why three individuals are usually assumed.
27094.m: At Laetoli, several human ancestors walked across the ash together.

27095.q: What was striking about the further footprints discovered at Laetoli in 2015?
a: One individual was much bigger than the ones known before.
They came from human ancestors on four legs.
They were only a few thousand years old.
They led into a big cave.
27095.e: About 150 metres from the old trackway, tracks of the same age from two individuals were found. One of them was much bigger than those known before.
27095.m: The human ancestors of Laetoli were of different sizes.

27096.q: How are the Laetoli footprints protected today?
a: They were covered with earth again.
They are under a glass roof.
They were taken to a museum.
27096.e: Taking them away would have been too expensive and too risky. So the tracks were buried again, which protects them best from wind, water and roots.
27096.m: The Laetoli tracks lie under the earth for protection.

27098.q: Which oldest stone tool culture is named after Olduvai Gorge?
27098.e: The simple pebble tools of this culture were first described in Olduvai Gorge. They are among the oldest known stone tools.
27098.m: The Oldowan culture is named after Olduvai Gorge.

a: A river cut it out over a long time
A meteorite struck it into the ground
People dug it for a canal
An earthquake tore it open in one night
27099.e: Water ate its way into the rock layers over hundreds of thousands of years. This uncovered old layers with fossils.
27099.m: A river washed out Olduvai Gorge.

27100.q: What nickname was the skull of Paranthropus boisei found in 1959 given because of its huge back teeth?
27100.e: Mary Leakey found the skull with very large back teeth and powerful jaws. That is why it was jokingly called “Nutcracker Man”.
27100.m: Paranthropus boisei had huge back teeth.

27101.q: About how deep is Olduvai Gorge at its deepest points?
27101.e: The gorge is up to about 100 metres deep. In its walls you can see rock layers from almost two million years.
27101.m: The walls of Olduvai Gorge show many old layers on top of each other.

27102.q: What was found in Olduvai Gorge?
a: Ancient stone tools and bones of human ancestors
27102.e: Fossils of several species of human ancestors and very old tools came to light in the gorge. The first fossils there were discovered in 1911.
27102.m: Traces of early humans were found in Olduvai Gorge.

27103.q: Near which famous crater is Olduvai Gorge?
27103.e: The gorge is about 20 kilometres north-west of the Ngorongoro Crater. Both belong to the landscape of the East African Rift.
27103.m: Olduvai Gorge is near the Ngorongoro Crater.

27104.q: What nickname does Olduvai Gorge have because of its many finds?
27104.e: Fossils of several species of human ancestors and humans, as well as very old tools, have been found in the gorge. That is why it is often called this.
27104.m: Olduvai Gorge is seen as the Cradle of Mankind.

27105.q: On which continent did Homo habilis live?
27105.e: All certain finds of Homo habilis come from East and Southern Africa. The earliest humans lived there.

27107.q: How did Homo habilis probably make its tools?
a: It struck stones against each other
It fired clay in an oven
27107.e: When struck, sharp flakes broke off the stone. These could be used for cutting and scraping.
27107.m: Homo habilis chipped tools out of stone.

27108.q: Based on the known finds, roughly when did Homo habilis live?
27108.e: All certain finds of Homo habilis are about 2.1 to 1.5 million years old. So it lived long before modern humans.
27108.m: Homo habilis lived around two million years ago.

27109.q: How big was the brain of Homo habilis compared with ours?
27109.e: Homo habilis had a bigger brain than the human ancestors before it. But people today have about twice as much.
27109.m: Homo habilis had a brain half the size of ours.

27110.q: Why was Homo habilis given this name?
a: Because stone tools were thought to be its work
Because it was very good at climbing
Because it was the first to make fire
27110.e: Simple stone tools lay in layers of the same age. People assumed this early human had made them.
27110.m: Homo habilis is seen as a toolmaker.

27111.q: Why do we know only a little about Homo habilis?
a: Mostly only single bones and teeth have been found
Only cave paintings of it have been found
No bones at all have been found
It only lived for a few years
27111.e: There is no complete skeleton of Homo habilis. Researchers have to work out a lot from jaws, teeth and parts of skulls.
27111.m: Only fragments of Homo habilis are known.

27112.q: What do cut marks on animal bones from the time of Homo habilis show?
a: That it cut meat off bones
That it kept animals as pets
That it wore bones as jewellery
27112.e: Fine notches on animal bones point to cuts made with sharp stones. So Homo habilis also ate meat.
27112.m: Cut marks show that Homo habilis ate meat.

27113.q: What does the name “Homo erectus” mean?
27113.e: The Latin “erectus” comes from “erigere”, which means to raise up. The name stresses the upright body.

27114.q: On which continent did Homo erectus first appear?
27114.e: The oldest finds of Homo erectus come from Africa. Later it spread as far as Asia.
27114.m: Homo erectus first appeared in Africa.

27115.q: What did Homo erectus manage as one of the first human species?
a: It travelled from Africa as far as Asia
27115.e: Finds from Java and China show that Homo erectus travelled long distances. Cities and writing only came much later.
27115.m: Homo erectus travelled from Africa to Asia.

27116.q: Under what name did Homo erectus finds from the 1920s at Zhoukoudian in China become known?
27116.e: The Zhoukoudian cave is near the Chinese capital. Davidson Black first called the finds Sinanthropus pekinensis.
27116.m: Peking Man belongs to Homo erectus.

27117.q: How did Homo erectus move around?
27117.e: Homo erectus had long legs and walked upright. That way it could cover long distances on foot.

27118.q: What did Homo erectus probably already use fire for?
27118.e: Traces of fire are about one million years old. Cooked food is easier to chew and digest.
27118.m: Homo erectus probably already used fire.

27119.q: Roughly how long did the species Homo erectus exist?
27119.e: The oldest finds are about 2 million years old, the youngest around 110,000 years. This means Homo erectus was successful for a very long time.
27119.m: Homo erectus existed for almost two million years.

27120.q: Roughly how tall were adult Homo erectus?
27120.e: Adult Homo erectus were about 1.45 to 1.80 metres tall and weighed 50 to 60 kilograms. Their body shape was already very similar to that of people today.
27120.m: Homo erectus was about as tall as people today.

27121.q: In which country was the Turkana Boy found?
27121.e: The site is about 5 kilometres west of Lake Turkana in northern Kenya. An almost complete skeleton of a young Homo erectus was discovered there.
27121.m: The Turkana Boy was found in Kenya.

a: The skeleton of a young early human
27122.e: The Turkana Boy is an almost complete skeleton of a boy of the species Homo erectus. He lived around 1.5 million years ago.
27122.m: The Turkana Boy is the skeleton of a young early human.

27123.q: What does the skeleton of the Turkana Boy show about Homo erectus?
a: It already had a body shape similar to ours
It was only as big as a cat
27123.e: The skeleton shows long legs and a slim, upright body. In this way Homo erectus was already very similar to modern humans.
27123.m: Homo erectus already had a human-like body shape.

27124.q: Roughly how old is the skeleton of the Turkana Boy?
27124.e: A detailed analysis gave an age of about 1.53 million years. Earlier it was estimated at around 1.6 million years.
27124.m: The Turkana Boy lived around one and a half million years ago.

27125.q: According to today's estimate, how old was the Turkana Boy when he died?
27125.e: At first people estimated 11 to 13 years. But growth lines in the tooth enamel showed that he was only about 8 to 9 years old.
27125.m: The Turkana Boy was still a child when he died.

27126.q: Which human species is the Turkana Boy usually assigned to?
27126.e: The skeleton shows a tall, slim body and a brain of around 880 cubic centimetres. Some experts also use the name Homo ergaster.
27126.m: The Turkana Boy was a young Homo erectus.

27127.q: Why is the Turkana Boy so important for research?
a: He is one of the most complete skeletons of an early human.
He is the oldest known prehuman.
The first ancient DNA was taken from him.
27127.e: 67 bones and 12 teeth were found, including many bones below the skull. For the first time, scientists could study the body of an early human in detail.
27127.m: The Turkana Boy is an especially complete skeleton.

27128.q: How can researchers tell that the Turkana Boy was still a child?
27128.e: In children, not all teeth have grown yet and the bones have not fully joined. This can also be seen in the skeleton.
27128.m: Teeth and bones reveal the age of a skeleton.

27129.q: What is the name of the culture whose typical tool is the hand axe?
27129.e: This culture is named after the site of Saint-Acheul in France. The hand axe is its key tool.
27129.m: The hand axe is the key tool of the Acheulean.

27130.q: What is special about the hand axe from Konso in Ethiopia, which is around 1.4 million years old?
27130.e: Almost all hand axes were knapped from stone. The piece from Konso, however, was made from a large animal bone.
27130.m: Hand axes were occasionally made of bone too.

27131.q: Roughly how long did the shape of the hand axe stay the same?
27131.e: Hand axes were made in much the same shape over a huge period of time. No other tool was in use for so long.
27131.m: The hand axe was in use for over a million years.

27132.q: What material are most hand axes made of?
27132.e: People mainly used fine-grained, hard rocks such as quartzite, volcanic rock or flint. They split well and gave sharp edges.
27132.m: Hand axes were usually knapped from hard stone.

27133.q: What is the hand axe called in French and in technical language?
27133.e: “Biface” means “two faces”. The word describes that the tool was worked on both sides.
27133.m: In technical language the hand axe is also called a biface.

27134.q: How long is a hand axe on average?
27134.e: Most hand axes are 10 to 25 centimetres long and sit well in the hand. But there are also much larger pieces.
27134.m: A hand axe is usually about as long as a hand.

27135.q: What was the hand axe probably used for?
a: as a versatile tool for cutting and chopping
only as a tip for arrows
only as jewellery around the neck
27135.e: Its exact purpose is not known for certain. Many experts think the hand axe was an all-purpose tool, for example for cutting up animals or working wood.
27135.m: The hand axe was probably an all-purpose tool of the Stone Age.

27136.e: The word comes from Latin: “bi” means two and “pes” means foot. Humans are the only living primates that move this way all the time.
27136.m: Bipedalism means walking on two legs.

27137.q: What big advantage did walking upright bring for the hands?
a: The hands became free for carrying and making things.
The hands became bigger and stronger.
The hands could now run better.
27137.e: If you walk on two legs, you do not need your hands to move around. So food, children or tools could be carried.

27138.q: How does the human head sit on the spine?
27138.e: In humans the spine meets the middle of the skull from below. So the head balances on the upright spine. In apes the head sits further forward.
27138.m: When walking upright, the head is balanced on the spine.

27139.q: What shape is the human spine when seen from the side?
27139.e: The double S shape cushions jolts when walking. It also brings the body's centre of gravity over the feet.
27139.m: The human spine has a double S shape.

27140.q: How is the human pelvis built compared with a chimpanzee's?
a: shorter and wider, like a bowl
longer and narrower, like a board
27140.e: The short, wide pelvis supports the internal organs from below. It also gives anchor points for muscles that keep the body stable when walking.
27140.m: A wide pelvis supports the upright body.

27141.q: What makes the human foot different from a chimpanzee's foot?
a: an arch and a big toe pointing forward
a big toe that spreads out for gripping
a flat foot without a heel
27141.e: The arch works like a spring, and the big toe pushes off forward when walking. Chimpanzees, by contrast, can grip with their feet.
27141.m: The human foot is built for walking, not gripping.

27142.q: On which continent were the oldest traces of human ancestors who walked on two legs found?
27142.e: The oldest finds of possible two-legged walkers come from Africa, for example a skull around 7 million years old from Chad. Africa is seen as the cradle of humankind.

27143.q: What hypothesis is there about the advantage of walking upright in the hot savannah?
a: The body offers less surface to the midday sun.
The body stores more water in the belly.
The body cannot be seen by predators.
The body no longer needs food.
27143.e: When you stand upright, the midday sun mainly hits your head and shoulders. There is also more cooling wind higher up.
27143.m: Standing upright protects against too much heat from the sun.

27145.q: What mainly supports the idea today that modern humans came from Africa?
a: Old fossils and comparisons of DNA
27145.e: The oldest fossils of Homo sapiens come from Africa. Comparisons of the DNA of people living today also point there.
27145.m: Fossils and DNA show that humans came from Africa.

27146.q: Roughly how many years ago did modern humans reach Australia?
27146.e: Finds from Australia show that people have lived there for at least around 50,000 years. Some dates go back even further.
27146.m: People have lived in Australia for tens of thousands of years.

27147.q: What did the first people on their way to Australia have to cross, even during the Ice Age?
27147.e: Even when sea levels were low, there was still open water between Southeast Asia and Australia. People had to cross it by boat or raft.
27147.m: Australia could only be reached by sea.

27148.q: According to current knowledge, how many years ago did larger groups of Homo sapiens leave Africa?
27148.e: Genetic data show that all people living outside Africa today go back to groups who left during this period. Earlier journeys mostly left no descendants.
27148.m: Homo sapiens left Africa in large numbers about 60,000 years ago.

27149.q: Across which land bridge did people reach America during the Ice Age?
a: Panama between North and South America
27149.e: Because a lot of water was locked up in ice during the Ice Age, the sea level was lower. As a result, the Bering Strait was dry land.
27149.m: The first Americans came across the land bridge of Beringia.

27150.q: On which continent did the common ancestors of all people living today live?
27150.e: Comparisons of DNA lead back to people who lived in Africa a long time ago. We are all descended from them.
27150.m: The ancestors of all people today lived in Africa.

27151.q: Across which sea, at its southern end, did early humans perhaps travel from Africa to Arabia?
27151.e: At the southern end of the Red Sea, Africa and Arabia lie close together. When the sea level was low, the strait was only a few kilometres wide.
27151.m: One possible route out of Africa led across the southern end of the Red Sea.

27152.q: Where is the genetic diversity of people today greatest?
27152.e: The longer people live in a place, the more genetic differences build up. The great diversity in Africa supports the idea that our species came from there.
27152.m: People in Africa are the most genetically diverse.

27153.q: In which present-day country was Homo floresiensis found?
27153.e: The island of Flores belongs to the Lesser Sunda Islands in Southeast Asia. The species is named after it.

27154.q: What nickname did Homo floresiensis get because of its small size?
27154.e: The nickname refers to the small characters in the books by J. R. R. Tolkien. It became very well known in the media.
27154.m: Homo floresiensis is often called the Hobbit.

27155.e: Researchers found the first skull in 2003. So it is a very recent discovery.
27155.m: Homo floresiensis was only discovered in 2003.

27156.q: Where were the bones of Homo floresiensis found?
a: In the ice of a glacier
27156.e: The bones lay in a limestone cave on the island of Flores. It is called Liang Bua.
27156.m: Homo floresiensis was found in a cave.

27157.q: Roughly how tall was Homo floresiensis?
27157.e: The skeleton LB1 and other bones show a height of about one metre. That made it smaller than most eight-year-old children today.
27157.m: Homo floresiensis was only about one metre tall.

27158.q: How big was the brain of Homo floresiensis compared with ours?
a: Much smaller, about like a chimpanzee's
27158.e: Its brain was only about a third the size of ours. Even so, it probably made stone tools.
27158.m: Homo floresiensis had a very small brain.

27159.q: Which people did Homo floresiensis perhaps live on Earth at the same time as?
a: The knights of the Middle Ages
27159.e: Homo floresiensis lived at least 60,000 years ago. Homo sapiens already existed then, but the Romans and knights were still a long way off.
27159.m: Homo floresiensis lived at the time of early Homo sapiens.

27160.q: Why did some animals and humans on the island of Flores become smaller over time?
a: Because there was little food on the island
Because it was very cold there
27160.e: On islands with little food, smaller bodies have an advantage. Over many generations, species can shrink as a result.
27160.m: On islands, species can become smaller over time.

27161.q: Which animals lived on Flores at the same time as Homo floresiensis?
27161.e: Bones of small elephants lay next to the human bones. Komodo dragons also lived on the island.
27161.m: Dwarf elephants once lived on Flores.

27162.q: In which region is the Denisova Cave?
27162.e: The cave is in the Altai Mountains in southern Siberia. Archaeologists have been studying it for decades.
27162.m: The Denisova Cave is in Siberia.

27163.q: From which find was the first DNA of the Denisovans obtained?
27163.e: The researchers studied a tiny finger bone from the Denisova Cave. Its DNA matched neither modern humans nor Neanderthals.
27163.m: The first Denisovan DNA came from a small finger bone.

27164.q: What did the DNA of a bone fragment from the Denisova Cave reveal about a girl in 2018?
a: Her mother was a Neanderthal, her father a Denisovan.
Both her parents were modern humans.
She was the daughter of two Homo erectus.
She was directly related to Lucy.
27164.e: The analysis showed a child whose parents belonged to two different kinds of humans. So Neanderthals and Denisovans met and had children together.
27164.m: Neanderthals and Denisovans had children together.

27165.q: How did researchers recognise the Denisovans as a separate kind of human?
27165.e: Only a few small bones and teeth of Denisovans exist. Only the study of their DNA showed that they were a separate kind of human.
27165.m: The Denisovans were discovered through their DNA.

27166.q: In which year did the Denisovans become known as a separate kind of human when their DNA was published?
27166.e: The results appeared in 2010 in the journal “Nature”. Before that, nobody knew about this kind of human.
27166.m: The Denisovans have only been known since 2010.

27167.q: What does the DNA of many people living in Oceania today show about the Denisovans?
a: They are descended directly from dinosaurs
27167.e: In some people in Oceania, a few percent of their DNA comes from Denisovans. So their ancestors once met them.
27167.m: Many people in Oceania carry Denisovan DNA.

27168.q: Which ability do many Tibetans probably owe to a gene variant from the Denisovans?
a: breathing more easily at high altitude
27168.e: A variant of the gene EPAS1 helps people cope with little oxygen. It probably reached the ancestors of the Tibetans through mixing with Denisovans.
27168.m: Tibetans inherited an adaptation to high altitude from the Denisovans.

27169.q: Where was a lower jaw found that was identified as Denisovan in 2019?
27169.e: The jaw comes from a karst cave at around 3280 metres above sea level in China. A monk had already found it in 1980.
27169.m: Denisovans also lived on the Tibetan Plateau.

27170.q: Where does the Denisova Cave get its name from?
27170.e: The Russian name roughly means “Denis's cave”. According to tradition, a hermit of that name once lived there.
27170.m: The Denisova Cave is named after a man called Denis.

27171.q: Why does the cave where the Neanderthal was found no longer exist today?
a: It was dug away by a quarry
It was flooded by a lake
27171.e: Limestone was quarried in the Neander Valley. The cave disappeared in the process, but more bones were later found in the old rubble.
27171.m: The cave in the Neander Valley was destroyed by a quarry.

27172.q: Who found the bones in the Neander Valley in 1856?
27172.e: Workers were clearing out a cave in the quarry and came across bones. They gave them to a teacher, who realised how important they were.
27172.m: Quarry workers found the Neanderthal in 1856.

27173.q: Where exactly were the Neanderthal's bones when they were discovered?
a: In the ice of a glacier
27173.e: The bones lay in the Kleine Feldhofer Grotte in the Neander Valley. The cave was later destroyed by limestone quarrying.
27173.m: The Neanderthal lay in a small cave.

27174.q: What did a teacher recognise about the bones from the Neander Valley?
a: They are human, but different from people today
They come from a cave bear
They are only a few years old
27174.e: The teacher Johann Carl Fuhlrott saw that the bones came from a human. But they were clearly different from people today.
27174.m: A teacher recognised the importance of the Neanderthal find.

27175.q: What is the scientific name of the Neanderthal?
27175.e: The name was proposed in 1864. “Homo” means human, and the second part refers to the Neander Valley.
27175.m: The scientific name of the Neanderthal is Homo neanderthalensis.

27176.q: Why did some researchers at first not believe that the Neanderthal was an early human?
a: They thought he was a sick modern human
They thought the bones were made of plaster
They thought he was a dinosaur
They thought he was an ape from a zoo
27176.e: The famous doctor Rudolf Virchow believed the unusual bones had been changed by disease. Only later was the find accepted as a separate kind of human.
27176.m: At first some people thought the Neanderthal was a sick human.

27177.q: In which present-day country is the Neander Valley?
27177.e: The Neander Valley is near Düsseldorf in Germany. It is named after the hymn writer Joachim Neander.
27177.m: The Neander Valley is in Germany.

27178.q: According to radiocarbon dating, roughly how old are the bones of the find Neanderthal 1?
27178.e: Measurements using the radiocarbon method gave an age of about 40,000 years. This makes the find one of the late Neanderthals.
27178.m: The Neanderthal from the Neander Valley lived about 40,000 years ago.

27179.q: In which country is the Lascaux cave?
27179.e: Lascaux is in the Dordogne in south-west France. There are many Old Stone Age sites there.

27180.q: Which animals are shown most often in Lascaux?
27180.e: Wild horses are the most common animals on the walls of Lascaux. There are also aurochs, deer, ibex and bison.
27180.m: Horses are the animals painted most often in Lascaux.

27181.q: Who discovered the Lascaux cave in 1940?
27181.e: Four teenagers came across the entrance in September 1940. They were amazed by the pictures on the walls.

a: A book about the Stone Age
27182.e: Because the real cave is closed, the most important parts were copied exactly. Lascaux II opened in 1983.
27182.m: Lascaux II is a replica of the cave.

27183.q: How long is the largest painted aurochs in Lascaux?
27183.e: The largest bull in the Hall of the Bulls measures 5.20 metres. It is one of the largest animal pictures of the Ice Age.
27183.m: The largest aurochs in Lascaux is over 5 metres long.

27185.q: Why is a mysterious animal in Lascaux called the “unicorn”?
a: Because of the straight lines on its head
Because it is painted all white
Because it is standing on a cloud
27185.e: The two straight lines on its head look like a horn. Nobody knows exactly which animal is meant.
27185.m: The “unicorn” of Lascaux is a mysterious animal.

27186.q: What else is there in Lascaux apart from paintings?
27186.e: Ice Age people scratched lines and animals into the rock with pointed stones. In one room alone there are over a thousand.
27186.m: There are also many engravings in Lascaux.

27188.q: What traces of a child were found in the Chauvet Cave?
27188.e: A trail over 70 metres long left by a child of about eight has survived in the clay floor.
27188.m: Footprints of a child survived in the Chauvet Cave.

27189.q: What can visitors see near the Chauvet Cave since 2015?
a: The original cave on a guided tour
27189.e: The real cave stays closed to protect it. The replica, “Grotte Chauvet 2”, is only a few kilometres away.
27189.m: The Chauvet Cave can only be visited as a replica.

27191.q: Which natural wonder is very close to the Chauvet Cave?
a: A natural rock arch over the river
27191.e: The Pont d'Arc is a mighty stone arch that the river Ardèche has carved into the rock. The village next to it is called Vallon-Pont-d'Arc.
27191.m: Next to the Chauvet Cave, a rock arch spans the river.

27192.q: Roughly how many pictures of animals and signs are there in the Chauvet Cave?
27192.e: The cave has over 400 wall pictures with a total of around 1000 painted and engraved animals and signs.
27192.m: The Chauvet Cave contains around 1000 pictures.

27193.q: Which bird is engraved into the rock in the Chauvet Cave?
27193.e: An owl is engraved on one wall. Pictures of birds are rare in Ice Age art.
27193.m: An owl is engraved in the Chauvet Cave.

27194.q: How were researchers able to work out the age of the black pictures in the Chauvet Cave?
27194.e: The black lines are made of charcoal. Charcoal contains carbon, whose age can be measured with the radiocarbon method.
27194.m: The age of charcoal drawings is measured with the radiocarbon method.

27196.q: How was the entrance to the Altamira cave discovered in 1868?
a: A man was looking for his hunting dog
27196.e: Modesto Cubillas was looking for his lost dog and came across the cave entrance.
27196.m: The Altamira cave was discovered while searching for a dog.

27197.q: Who first noticed the pictures on the ceiling of Altamira in 1879?
27197.e: Marcelino Sanz de Sautuola was examining the floor of the cave. His little daughter María looked up and discovered the animal pictures.
27197.m: A child discovered the ceiling paintings of Altamira.

27198.q: Which animals on the ceiling of Altamira are especially famous?
27198.e: The ceiling shows a group of coloured bison. There are also deer, horses and wild boar.
27198.m: Altamira is famous for its painted bison.

27199.q: Which colours are most common in the bison of Altamira?
27199.e: The painters made red from ochre and black from charcoal. Blue and green paints were unknown in the Ice Age.
27199.m: The bison of Altamira are painted in red and black.

27200.q: What nickname is the Altamira cave often given?
a: Sistine Chapel of the Stone Age
Eiffel Tower of the Stone Age
27200.e: The painted ceiling is reminiscent of the famous ceiling painting in the Sistine Chapel in Rome.
27200.m: Altamira is known as the Sistine Chapel of the Stone Age.

27201.q: How did the painters in Altamira use the shape of the cave ceiling?
a: They painted animals on bulges in the rock
27201.e: The painters placed the bison on natural bulges in the rock. This makes the bodies look almost three-dimensional.
27201.m: In Altamira the animals look three-dimensional thanks to the bulges in the rock.

27202.q: Roughly how old are the paintings of Altamira?
27202.e: The pictures were made in the Ice Age many thousands of years ago. At that time people still hunted bison and wild horses.
27202.m: The pictures of Altamira date from the Ice Age.

27203.q: Why are visitors no longer allowed to visit the original Altamira cave freely?
a: Breath and mould damaged the pictures
The cave belongs to a private person
The pictures were taken to a museum
27203.e: The many visitors changed the climate in the cave with their warm breath, and mould formed on the pictures. Today you can see a replica in the museum next door.
27203.m: Altamira is closed to protect the pictures.

27204.q: On which river is the site where the Venus of Willendorf was found?
27204.e: Willendorf is in the Wachau, a valley on the Danube.

27206.q: Roughly how old is the Venus of Willendorf?
27206.e: The figure dates from the Old Stone Age. Its age is estimated at about 29,500 years.
27206.m: The Venus of Willendorf is around 29,500 years old.

27207.q: From which period does the Venus of Willendorf date?
27207.e: The figure is around 29,500 years old. At that time people lived as hunter-gatherers in the Old Stone Age.
27207.m: The Venus of Willendorf dates from the Old Stone Age.

27208.q: Traces of which colour can still be found on the Venus of Willendorf?
27208.e: Remains of red ochre have survived on the figure. So it was originally painted red.
27208.m: The Venus of Willendorf was once painted red.

27209.q: What can be seen on the head of the Venus of Willendorf instead of a face?
27209.e: The face is not carved. The whole head is covered with rows that look like curls of hair or a cap.
27209.m: The Venus of Willendorf has no carved face.

27211.q: What are small female figures from the Old Stone Age often called?
27211.e: Researchers name such figures after the Roman goddess Venus. They have been found all over Europe, for example in Willendorf in Austria.
27211.m: Female figures from the Old Stone Age are called Venus figurines.

27212.q: What does the figure of the Lion Man show?
a: A being with a lion's head
A hunter wearing a lion skin
27212.e: The figure has a lion's head and an upright human body. It combines animal and human.
27212.m: The Lion Man is half lion and half human.

27213.q: What material is the Lion Man carved from?
27213.e: The figure was carved from a mammoth's tusk. With stone tools this was very hard work.
27213.m: The Lion Man is made of mammoth ivory.

27214.q: In which region was the Lion Man found?
27214.e: The figure lay in the Hohlenstein-Stadel cave in the Lone valley in Baden-Württemberg.
27214.m: The Lion Man comes from the Swabian Jura.

27215.q: Which animal that lived in Europe during the Ice Age was probably the model for the Lion Man's head?
27215.e: Cave lions lived in Europe during the Ice Age. People knew them and showed them in their art.
27215.m: The Lion Man has the head of a cave lion.

27216.q: How tall is the Lion Man?
27216.e: The figure is 31.1 centimetres tall. For an ivory figure from the Ice Age, that is very large.
27216.m: The Lion Man is about 31 centimetres tall.

27217.q: Roughly how old is the Lion Man?
27217.e: The figure is between about 35,000 and 41,000 years old. It is one of the oldest works of art made by humans.
27217.m: The Lion Man is about 40,000 years old.

27218.q: In which city is the Lion Man on display today?
27218.e: The original is in the Museum Ulm. The excavator Robert Wetzel gave his finds to the city.
27218.m: The Lion Man is in the Museum Ulm.

27219.q: What condition was the Lion Man in when it was dug up?
27219.e: The figure consisted of hundreds of fragments. Only in 1969 did Joachim Hahn recognise what it showed, and later it was put back together several times.
27219.m: The Lion Man was put together from many fragments.

27220.q: Under which title has the site of the Lion Man been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2017?
a: Caves and Ice Age Art in the Swabian Jura
27220.e: In 2017 six caves in the Swabian Jura were added to the World Heritage list. Some of the oldest works of art in the world were found in them.
27220.m: The Ice Age caves of the Swabian Jura have been World Heritage since 2017.

27221.q: Roughly how old are the oldest flutes from the Swabian Jura?
27221.e: The flutes date from the time when modern humans arrived in Europe. They are about 35,000 to 43,000 years old.
27221.m: The oldest flutes are about 40,000 years old.

27222.q: Which other material did Ice Age people also make flutes from, even though it was much harder?
27222.e: A piece of tusk had to be split lengthways, hollowed out and joined back together tightly.
27222.m: Some Ice Age flutes are made of mammoth ivory.

27223.q: How did people play different notes on a bone flute?
a: By covering and opening finger holes
By hitting it with a stick
27223.e: Holes were drilled into the flute. Depending on which holes you cover with your fingers, a different note sounds.
27223.m: Finger holes are used to play different notes.

27224.q: What do the bone flutes of the Ice Age prove?
a: People already made music back then
27224.e: The flutes are among the oldest musical instruments in the world. So music was part of life very early on.
27224.m: People were already making music in the Ice Age.

27225.q: What is the flute from Hohle Fels made of?
27225.e: The flute was carved from the hollow wing bone of a large bird, a griffon vulture. Bird bones are hollow inside, so they are well suited.
27225.m: The flute from Hohle Fels is made from a bird bone.

27226.q: Roughly how long is the flute from Hohle Fels?
27226.e: The flute is just under 22 centimetres long, so about as long as a 20-centimetre school ruler.
27226.m: The flute from Hohle Fels is about 22 centimetres long.

27227.q: Why is the supposed Neanderthal flute from the Divje Babe cave in Slovenia disputed?
a: The holes could be bite marks
It was bought in a shop
27227.e: The bone comes from a young cave bear. Many researchers think the holes were made by the teeth of a predator.
27227.m: The flute from Divje Babe may not be a flute at all.

27228.q: What was a spear-thrower used for?
a: To throw spears further and harder
To pull fish out of the water
27228.e: The spear-thrower lengthens the arm like a lever. This makes the spear fly faster and further and hit with more force.
27228.m: A spear-thrower made spears fly further.

27229.q: Which hunting weapon later largely replaced the spear-thrower in Europe?
27229.e: Towards the end of the Ice Age, bows and arrows took over. They let people shoot more quietly and more accurately.
27229.m: Bows and arrows later replaced the spear-thrower.

27230.q: Where did people still use the spear-thrower until modern times?
27230.e: Aboriginal Australians hunted with the spear-thrower into modern times. They call it a woomera.
27230.m: In Australia the spear-thrower was used into modern times.

27231.q: From which period do the oldest known spear-throwers in Europe date?
a: From the late Old Stone Age
27231.e: The oldest surviving spear-throwers in Europe are around 17,000 to 20,000 years old. They date from the late Old Stone Age.
27231.m: Spear-throwers have existed in Europe since the late Old Stone Age.

27232.q: Who was the first to dig in the Kesslerloch in 1873?
27232.e: The secondary school teacher Konrad Merk began the excavation in December 1873 and published the results in 1875.
27232.m: A teacher was the first to dig in the Kesslerloch.

27233.q: How many years ago did reindeer hunters use the Kesslerloch?
27233.e: Hunters of the Magdalenian culture used the cave as a shelter about 15,000 to 11,000 years ago.
27233.m: Reindeer hunters used the Kesslerloch about 15,000 years ago.

27234.q: What turned out to be true about the engravings of a fox and a bear from the Kesslerloch?
a: They were the oldest in the world
They were made by Ice Age children
27234.e: The pictures were made later, in 1875. A researcher realised that they had been copied from a children's book.
27234.m: Two drawings from the Kesslerloch were fakes.

27235.q: Which find from the Kesslerloch is early proof of dogs as pets?
a: A piece of a dog's jaw
A dog's grave with grave goods
27235.e: A piece of a dog's upper jaw is around 14,000 to 15,000 years old. It is one of the oldest signs of domestic dogs in Central Europe.
27235.m: One of the oldest dog bones in Central Europe was found in the Kesslerloch.

27236.q: Bones of how many animal species were found in the Kesslerloch?
27236.e: Bones of 53 animal species were found, including mammoth, reindeer, ibex and chamois.
27236.m: Bones of over 50 animal species were found in the Kesslerloch.

27237.q: Where does the Kesslerloch get its name from?
a: From the round shape of the cave
27237.e: Travelling tinkers, known in German as “Kessler”, used to repair cooking pots in the cave.
27237.m: The Kesslerloch is named after the tinkers.

27238.q: In which canton is the Kesslerloch cave?
27238.e: The Kesslerloch is near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen. It is one of the most important Ice Age sites in Switzerland.
27238.m: The Kesslerloch is in the canton of Schaffhausen.

27239.q: What is the decorated perforated baton from the Kesslerloch carved from?
27239.e: The reindeer hunters carved tools and works of art from antler. They did not yet know about metal.
27239.m: The perforated baton from the Kesslerloch is made of reindeer antler.

27240.q: What were the pendants found in the Kesslerloch made of?
27240.e: The reindeer hunters wore pendants made of shells, snail shells, animal teeth and jet. They did not yet know about metal.
27240.m: The reindeer hunters wore jewellery made of shells and teeth.

27241.q: In which canton are the Wildkirchli caves?
27241.e: The caves lie below the Ebenalp in the canton of Appenzell Innerrhoden.
27241.m: The Wildkirchli is in Appenzell Innerrhoden.

27242.q: What was found during excavations at the Wildkirchli?
a: Stone tools and cave bear bones
27242.e: From 1904 onwards, stone tools and many animal bones were found at the Wildkirchli. Most of the bones come from cave bears.
27242.m: Stone tools and cave bear bones were found at the Wildkirchli.

27243.q: Which people left stone tools at the Wildkirchli?
27243.e: The worked stones are several tens of thousands of years old. They show that Neanderthals moved around this area.
27243.m: Neanderthals left tools at the Wildkirchli.

27244.q: Why were the finds at the Wildkirchli a sensation at the time?
a: First proof of Stone Age people in the Alps
27244.e: Until then, people believed that Old Stone Age humans had avoided the Alps. The Wildkirchli proved the opposite.
27244.m: The Wildkirchli showed that Stone Age people were in the Alps.

27245.q: Who lived in the Wildkirchli from 1658 to 1853?
27245.e: Several hermits lived in the caves one after another and looked after the cave chapel. That is where the name Wildkirchli, meaning “little wild church”, comes from.
27245.m: Hermits used to live in the Wildkirchli.

27246.q: What is there in one of the Wildkirchli caves?
27246.e: There is a chapel in the altar cave. That is where the name Wildkirchli, meaning “little wild church”, comes from.
27246.m: There is a cave chapel in the Wildkirchli.

27247.q: Which well-known mountain inn stands against a rock face near the Wildkirchli?
27247.e: The Aescher mountain inn clings to the rock face below the Ebenalp. It belongs to the Wildkirchli Foundation.
27247.m: The Aescher inn stands near the Wildkirchli.

27248.q: How many caves make up the Wildkirchli?
27248.e: The Wildkirchli consists of three limestone caves with a total length of around 150 metres. A hiking path runs through one of them.
27248.m: The Wildkirchli consists of three caves.

27249.q: Why are very many cave bear bones found in some caves?
a: Many died during their winter rest
27249.e: Weak and old animals often did not survive the winter in the cave. Over thousands of years, many bones built up.
27249.m: Many cave bears died in their winter cave.

27250.q: What did people in the past think the large skulls of cave bears were?
27250.e: Because people did not know these animals, they thought the skulls were the remains of dragons. That is why some caves have names like Dragon's Cave.
27250.m: Cave bear skulls were once thought to be dragon skulls.

27251.q: What does the Latin species name “spelaeus” mean in the cave bear's name Ursus spelaeus?
27251.e: “Ursus” means bear and “spelaeus” means “living in caves”. The name fits because its bones are found mainly in caves.

27252.q: How can you easily recognise the skull of a cave bear?
27252.e: In the cave bear the forehead rises steeply behind the snout. In the brown bear the profile is flatter.
27252.m: The cave bear had a steep forehead.

27253.q: What did people once suspect because of the bear skulls in the Drachenloch above Vättis?
a: A bear cult of Stone Age people
27253.e: The excavators believed people had placed the skulls in stone boxes on purpose. Today most researchers think the arrangement happened naturally.
27253.m: A bear cult in the Drachenloch is now thought unlikely.

27254.q: What did cave bears mainly eat?
27254.e: Studies of their teeth and bones show that cave bears mainly ate plants. They were bigger than today's brown bears.

27255.q: Which traces of cave bears have survived on the floor of the Chauvet Cave?
a: Hollows where they spent the winter
27255.e: Hollows can be seen in the clay floor where cave bears had their winter rest. Prints of their paws have also survived.
27255.m: Cave bears left sleeping hollows in the Chauvet Cave.

27256.q: What was the horn of the woolly rhinoceros made of?
27256.e: Rhino horns are made of keratin, the same material as hair and fingernails. That is why they have rarely survived.
27256.m: The horn of the woolly rhinoceros was made of keratin.

27257.q: In which landscape did the woolly rhinoceros mainly live?
27257.e: The woolly rhinoceros lived in the mammoth steppe, a cold, dry grassland without many trees.
27257.m: The woolly rhinoceros lived in the cold steppe.

27258.q: How do researchers know what the woolly rhinoceros looked like?
a: From well-preserved finds and cave pictures
From photos taken in the Ice Age
27258.e: Woolly rhinos have survived with skin and hair in frozen ground and in earth wax. Ice Age people also painted them on cave walls.
27258.m: Finds and cave pictures show what the woolly rhinoceros looked like.

27260.q: What did the woolly rhinoceros probably use its front horn for in winter?
a: To drill holes in the ice
27260.e: The front horn often shows heavy signs of wear. The animal probably used it to push snow aside to reach plants.
27260.m: The woolly rhinoceros pushed snow aside with its horn.

27261.q: How long could the front horn of the woolly rhinoceros grow?
27261.e: The front horn grew up to 90 centimetres long, and even longer when measured along the curve.
27261.m: The front horn of the woolly rhinoceros was up to 90 centimetres long.

27262.q: Roughly how heavy was an adult woolly rhinoceros?
27262.e: A woolly rhinoceros weighed about 1.5 to 2.9 tonnes. That is as much as a large car or more.
27262.m: A woolly rhinoceros weighed around 2 tonnes.

27263.q: What did reindeer hunters need the sinews of the animals they killed for?
27263.e: Dried sinews are very strong. People used them to sew clothes and to tie points onto spears.
27263.m: Reindeer sinews were used as thread.

27264.q: Why are so many reindeer bones found at campsites from the late Old Stone Age?
a: Reindeer were the most important prey
27264.e: The reindeer hunters used almost every part of the animal: meat, fur, bones, antlers and sinews. That is why so many bones lie at their campsites.
27264.m: Reindeer were the most important prey in the late Old Stone Age.

27265.q: Which famous cave in the canton of Schaffhausen was a campsite of reindeer hunters?
27265.e: The Kesslerloch is near Thayngen. Many tools and works of art made by reindeer hunters of the late Old Stone Age were found there.
27265.m: Reindeer hunters lived in the Kesslerloch near Thayngen.

27266.q: What were the perforated batons made of reindeer antler probably used for?
27266.e: A perforated baton is a piece of antler with a large hole. Many researchers believe it was used to straighten heated spear shafts.
27266.m: Perforated batons were probably used to straighten spear shafts.

27267.q: How could people get reindeer antlers even without hunting?
a: Reindeer shed their antlers every year
They bought them at the market
Antlers turned up as stones in river sand
27267.e: Reindeer lose their antlers every year and grow new ones. The shed antlers could be collected.
27267.m: Reindeer shed their antlers every year.

27268.q: What did the reindeer hunters do when the reindeer herds moved on?
27268.e: Reindeer travel long distances over the year. The hunters moved with them and set up camp wherever the animals were.

27269.q: Why did reindeer disappear from the area of Switzerland at the end of the Ice Age?
a: It got warmer and forest spread
27269.e: With the warmer climate, forests grew and the open cold steppe disappeared. The reindeer moved north, where it stayed cold.
27269.m: As it got warmer, the reindeer moved north.

27270.q: How far did the Rhine Glacier advance in the last Ice Age?
27270.e: The Rhine Glacier filled the basin of Lake Constance and, at its greatest extent, reached Schaffhausen.
27270.m: The Rhine Glacier reached as far as Schaffhausen.

27271.q: Which river is the last Ice Age in the Alpine region named after?
27271.e: Researchers named the ice ages of the Alps after rivers in the Bavarian Alpine foothills. The most recent one is called the Würm glaciation.
27271.m: The last Ice Age is named after the river Würm.

27272.q: Which glacier did the Rhône Glacier join up with in the Bern area?
27272.e: In the Bern region, the Rhône Glacier and the Aare Glacier met and flowed on together.
27272.m: The Rhône and Aare Glaciers met near Bern.

27273.q: Which glacier shaped the basin of Lake Biel and Lake Neuchâtel?
27273.e: A tongue of the Rhône Glacier flowed north-east along the foot of the Jura and scoured out the basins of the two lakes.
27273.m: The Rhône Glacier shaped Lake Biel and Lake Neuchâtel.

27274.q: By how much was the average annual temperature in Switzerland lower than today during the greatest glaciation?
27274.e: Around 20,000 years ago, the annual average was about 12 to 15 degrees colder than today. Summers were around 8 to 10 degrees cooler.
27274.m: During the greatest glaciation, Switzerland was around 12 to 15 degrees colder than today.

27275.q: What are the long hills shaped by glaciers called, for example in the Zurich Oberland?
27275.e: Drumlins are streamlined hills that formed under flowing ice. Their long axis shows the direction in which the glacier flowed.
27275.m: Drumlins are hills shaped by a glacier.

27276.q: Where do many large gravel deposits in the Swiss Plateau come from?
27276.e: The meltwater rivers in front of the glaciers deposited huge amounts of gravel and sand. Today this gravel is dug up for building.
27276.m: Much of the gravel in the Swiss Plateau comes from Ice Age meltwater.

27277.q: How did researchers realise that glaciers used to be much bigger?
a: From erratic boulders and moraines far from the Alps
From photos from the Stone Age
27277.e: In the Swiss Plateau there are large rocks from the Alps, called erratic boulders. Only huge glaciers could have carried them so far.
27277.m: Erratic boulders and moraines show how far the glaciers reached.

27278.q: What holds back Lake Zurich at its lower end near the city of Zurich?
a: A moraine of the Linth Glacier
27278.e: As it retreated, the Linth Glacier stayed near Zurich for a while and left a moraine ridge. The lake water collected behind it.
27278.m: Lake Zurich is held back by a moraine.

27279.q: What shape does the area called the “Fertile Crescent” have on the map?
27279.e: The area curves in an arc from the Levant on the Mediterranean across south-eastern Anatolia to the Persian Gulf. On the map it looks like a crescent moon.
27279.m: The Fertile Crescent has the shape of a crescent moon.

27280.q: Which American archaeologist coined the term “Fertile Crescent” around 1916?
27280.e: The Egyptologist James Henry Breasted used the expression “Fertile Crescent” in his books. The name caught on all over the world.
27280.m: James Henry Breasted came up with the name Fertile Crescent.
