27281.q: Between which two rivers does Mesopotamia, the eastern part of the Fertile Crescent, lie?
27281.e: Mesopotamia means “land between the rivers”. This refers to the Euphrates and Tigris in present-day Iraq.
27281.m: Mesopotamia lies between the Euphrates and Tigris.

27282.q: What began in the Fertile Crescent around 11,000 to 12,000 years ago?
27282.e: Here people began growing grain and keeping animals for the first time. This change is called the Neolithic Revolution.
27282.m: Farming and keeping livestock began in the Fertile Crescent.

27283.q: Which archaeologist coined the term “Neolithic Revolution”?
27283.e: The Australian archaeologist Vere Gordon Childe described the change to farming and settled life as a revolution. The term is still used today.
27283.m: Vere Gordon Childe spoke of the Neolithic Revolution.

27284.q: Which pulse is one of the first crops of the Fertile Crescent?
27284.e: Lentils, peas and chickpeas were already grown there in the New Stone Age. Soya beans, peanuts and French beans come from Asia or America.
27284.m: The lentil is one of the oldest crops.

27285.q: What is the name of the culture in the Levant whose people lived in permanent settlements even before farming?
27285.e: From about 12,500 BC, the Natufian people partly lived in one place and harvested wild grain. They are seen as forerunners of the first farmers.
27285.m: The Natufian people settled down before they became farmers.

27286.q: Which two animal species were among the first farm animals in the Fertile Crescent?
27286.e: Goats and sheep were already kept there around 10,000 to 11,000 years ago. They provided meat, milk and skins.
27286.m: Goats and sheep are among the oldest farm animals.

27287.q: What is the western part of the Fertile Crescent on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean called?
27287.e: The Levant covers roughly the area of present-day Israel, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria. Some of the earliest farmers lived here.
27287.m: The Levant is on the eastern coast of the Mediterranean.

27288.q: Roughly how old are the oldest structures at Göbekli Tepe?
27288.e: The oldest buildings were made around 9500 BC. That makes them much older than the pyramids in Egypt.
27288.m: Göbekli Tepe is over 11,000 years old.

27289.q: What shape are the large stone pillars of Göbekli Tepe?
27289.e: The pillars look like a big T. Arms and hands are carved on some of them, so they are thought to be very simplified human figures.
27289.m: There are T-shaped pillars at Göbekli Tepe.

27290.q: According to current knowledge, who built Göbekli Tepe?
27290.e: When it was built, there was not yet any real farming there. The builders were people who lived by hunting and gathering.

27291.q: What did the builders of Göbekli Tepe use to work the large stone pillars?
27291.e: At the time it was built, people did not yet know about metal. They carved the pillars out of the rock with hard stone tools.
27291.m: Göbekli Tepe was built with stone tools.

27292.q: What is shown in relief on many of the pillars of Göbekli Tepe?
27292.e: The pillars show foxes, snakes, wild boar and birds, among other things. Writing did not yet exist at that time.
27292.m: The pillars of Göbekli Tepe show wild animals.

27293.q: Why is Göbekli Tepe a UNESCO World Heritage Site today?
a: It is one of the oldest large structures built by humans
It is the largest castle in Europe
27293.e: The site is over 11,000 years old and so much older than the pyramids. It has been World Heritage since 2018.
27293.m: Göbekli Tepe is one of the oldest structures in the world.

27294.q: How are the large pillars of Göbekli Tepe usually arranged?
27294.e: The pillars form round to oval enclosures surrounded by walls. Two especially large pillars stand in the middle of each.
27294.m: At Göbekli Tepe the pillars stand in circular enclosures.

27295.q: What does the Turkish name Göbekli Tepe roughly mean in English?
27295.e: “Tepe” means hill and “göbek” means belly or navel. So the name is often translated as “Potbelly Hill”.

27296.q: What kind of rock did the builders carve the pillars of Göbekli Tepe from?
27296.e: The pillars were cut directly from the limestone rock in the area. Traces of the quarries can still be seen today.
27296.m: The pillars of Göbekli Tepe are made of limestone.

27297.q: Roughly how old is the settlement of Çatalhöyük?
27297.e: Çatalhöyük existed from about 7400 to 6000 BC. It is one of the oldest large settlements in the world.

27298.q: What did the people of Çatalhöyük mainly build their houses from?
27298.e: The walls were made of air-dried mud bricks. Inside they were plastered with clay and often painted.
27298.m: The houses of Çatalhöyük were made of mud bricks.

27299.q: Where did the people of Çatalhöyük often bury their dead?
a: Under the floor of their houses
27299.e: The dead were buried under the platforms and floors of the living rooms. So the living lived directly above their ancestors.
27299.m: In Çatalhöyük the dead lay under the floor of the house.

27300.q: Which animal parts did the people of Çatalhöyük often fix to the walls?
27300.e: In many rooms, bulls' horns set into clay were found. The bull was clearly an important symbol.
27300.m: In Çatalhöyük bulls' horns decorated the walls.

27301.q: How do archaeologists find out how people lived in Çatalhöyük?
a: They dig up the remains of the houses
27301.e: There is no writing from the time of Çatalhöyük. But walls, graves, tools and bones reveal a lot about life there.
27301.m: Excavations show how people lived in Çatalhöyük.

27302.q: How did the mound on which Çatalhöyük lies form?
a: From the remains of many houses built on top of each other
27302.e: Old mud houses were knocked down and new ones built on top. Over many centuries, a mound of settlement layers grew.
27302.m: The mound of Çatalhöyük is made of the remains of old houses.

27303.q: Which black volcanic glass was an important raw material in Çatalhöyük?
27303.e: Obsidian comes from volcanoes in central Anatolia. It was used to make very sharp blades and even mirrors.

27304.q: Which animals sit next to the famous clay figure of a woman from Çatalhöyük?
27304.e: The seated woman of Çatalhöyük rests her hands on two big cats, probably leopards. The figure is now in a museum in Ankara.
27304.m: The female figure from Çatalhöyük sits between big cats.

27305.q: Why is Çatalhöyük a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
a: It is one of the oldest large settlements in the world
It is the current capital of Turkey
27305.e: Çatalhöyük shows very well how the first farmers lived together around 9000 years ago. That is why it has been on the World Heritage list since 2012.
27305.m: Çatalhöyük is World Heritage as one of the oldest large settlements.

27306.q: What is special about the location of the city of Jericho?
a: It lies far below sea level
27306.e: Jericho lies in the Jordan Valley around 250 metres below sea level. It is considered the lowest city in the world.
27306.m: Jericho lies far below sea level.

27307.q: Which stone structure was built in Jericho around 8000 BC?
27307.e: The Tower of Jericho is around 8.5 metres high and has a staircase inside. It is considered one of the oldest stone structures in the world.
27307.m: The Tower of Jericho is over 10,000 years old.

27308.q: How did people make a living in New Stone Age Jericho?
27308.e: Thanks to the spring, people could grow grain. They were among the first farmers in the world.

27309.q: What did the people of New Stone Age Jericho do with some of the skulls of their dead?
a: They shaped faces on them with plaster
They threw them into the river
They built them into the tower
27309.e: Some skulls were modelled over with plaster and given shells as eyes. This created lifelike faces.
27309.m: In Jericho faces were modelled onto skulls.

27310.q: Why were people able to live permanently in Jericho so early?
27310.e: The spring of Ain es-Sultan still provides a lot of water today. In the dry region it made the oasis fertile.
27310.m: Jericho grew up at a spring with plenty of water.

27311.q: What is Jericho often known for in rankings?
a: As one of the oldest cities in the world
As the highest city in the world
As the biggest city in the world
As the northernmost city in the world
27311.e: People have lived on the site of Jericho for over 10,000 years. That is why the city is one of the oldest continuously inhabited places.
27311.m: Jericho is one of the oldest cities in the world.

27312.q: How did the settlement mound of ancient Jericho form?
a: From the remains of many settlements on top of each other
From sand blown in by the wind
27312.e: Again and again, people built on the ruins of older houses. Over time this created a mound called a tell.
27312.m: A settlement mound is made of many settlement layers.

27313.q: In which area is the city of Jericho today?
27313.e: Jericho is in the West Bank, near the Jordan and the Dead Sea. The city is administered by the Palestinian Authority.
27313.m: Jericho is in the West Bank.

27314.q: What surrounded the New Stone Age settlement of Jericho?
27314.e: A stone wall with a ditch in front of it ran around the settlement. It is one of the oldest walls in the world.
27314.m: Early Jericho had a stone wall.

27315.q: What was found next to a man and a woman in a grave near Bonn that is around 14,000 years old?
27315.e: In the double grave of Bonn-Oberkassel, a dog lay with the people. The find shows a close bond between people and dogs.
27315.m: A dog was buried with people as long as 14,000 years ago.

a: Wild forms become domestic animals over generations
A single wild animal is tamed
Wild animals are kept in a zoo
Wild plants are gathered in the forest
27316.e: In domestication, animals or plants change over many generations because humans choose which ones to breed. A single tamed animal is not yet domesticated.

27317.q: How can researchers tell from old bones that they belong to a dog and not a wolf?
a: By the shorter snout and smaller teeth
27317.e: Early dogs usually had a shorter snout and smaller, more closely spaced teeth than wolves. Today DNA analysis also helps with identification.
27317.m: Dogs usually have shorter snouts than wolves.

27318.q: Thanks to extra genes, what can dogs digest better than wolves?
27318.e: Dogs often have more copies of a gene for digesting starch. This fits with the fact that they ate leftover grain from farmers.
27318.m: Dogs digest starch better than wolves.

27319.q: Where was evidence found of sled dogs that lived around 9500 years ago?
27319.e: On the Siberian island of Zhokhov, dog bones and parts of sledges were found. The dogs were clearly already being bred to pull sledges at that time.
27319.m: There were sled dogs in Siberia very early on.

27320.q: Which animals is the dingo in Australia descended from?
a: From domestic dogs that people brought with them
27320.e: The dingo is descended from dogs that came to Australia with people a few thousand years ago. There they went back to living in the wild.
27320.m: The dingo is descended from domestic dogs.

27321.q: In which region was einkorn first grown?
27321.e: Einkorn was domesticated over 10,000 years ago in the Fertile Crescent, probably in the area of present-day south-eastern Turkey. From there it came to Europe.
27321.m: Einkorn comes from the Near East.

27322.q: What changed in einkorn when people grew it and kept choosing the seed?
a: The grains no longer fell off by themselves
The plant turned into a tree
The plant no longer needed water
27322.e: In wild grain, the ripe grains fall off by themselves. The farmers mainly harvested ears that kept their grains and sowed these again.
27322.m: Domesticated grain keeps its grains on the ear.

27323.q: Remains of which grain were found in the stomach of the glacier mummy Ötzi?
27323.e: Besides meat, Ötzi's last meal also contained einkorn. This shows that his community farmed.
27323.m: Ötzi ate einkorn before he died.

27324.q: Which present-day grain, used to make pasta, came directly from emmer?
27324.e: Durum wheat developed from domesticated emmer. Its semolina is used to make spaghetti and other pasta.
27324.m: Durum wheat is descended from emmer.

27325.q: Which grain came from a cross between emmer and a wild grass?
27325.e: Spelt developed from a natural cross between emmer and a wild grass. Spelt is still widely grown in Switzerland today.
27325.m: Spelt is a descendant of emmer.

27326.q: Which kind of wheat was the most important grain for bread and beer in ancient Egypt?
27326.e: In the Nile valley the Egyptians mainly grew emmer and barley. They baked bread and brewed beer from emmer.
27326.m: Emmer was very important in ancient Egypt.

27327.q: Where does wild emmer, the ancestor of cultivated emmer, grow?
27327.e: Wild emmer was found in 1906 in the north of present-day Israel. It shows that wheat comes from the Near East.
27327.m: Wild emmer grows in the Near East.

27328.q: What is Linear Pottery, the first farming culture of Central Europe, named after?
a: The band-shaped decorations on its pots
27328.e: The pots of this culture are decorated with engraved bands of lines. Linear Pottery existed from about 5500 to 4900 BC.
27328.m: Linear Pottery is named after its bands of lines.

27329.q: Where were the oldest known pottery vessels in the world found?
27329.e: In China and Japan, hunter-gatherers were already making clay pots around 20,000 years ago. That was long before farming.
27329.m: The oldest pottery comes from East Asia.

27330.q: What is the Bell Beaker culture named after?
a: Cups shaped like an upside-down bell
27330.e: The typical drinking cups of this culture look like a bell turned upside down. The culture spread across large parts of Europe.
27330.m: Bell beakers look like upside-down bells.

27331.q: How did the people of the Corded Ware culture decorate their pots?
a: They pressed cords into the damp clay
They painted them with gold paint
They stuck pieces of glass on them
27331.e: Before firing, twisted cords were pressed into the soft clay. The prints gave the culture its name.
27331.m: Corded Ware is decorated with cord prints.

27332.q: Where did the potter's wheel first appear?
27332.e: In Mesopotamia, potters were already using turning wheels in the 5th and 4th millennia BC. In Switzerland it only became common thousands of years later.
27332.m: The potter's wheel comes from the Near East.

27333.q: Why do pottery fragments help archaeologists to date a site?
a: Shapes and decorations changed over time
Fragments change colour the same way every year
27333.e: Every culture had typical pot shapes and patterns. So the fragments show which period a layer comes from.
27333.m: Pottery fragments reveal the age of a layer.

27334.q: What did New Stone Age pottery in Europe lack compared with many later pots?
27334.e: New Stone Age pots were unglazed and so let some liquid through. Glazes only appeared in Europe much later.
27334.m: New Stone Age pots had no glaze.

27335.q: Why have fabrics from the lake-dwelling settlements in Switzerland survived until today?
a: They lay in damp ground without air
They were mended again and again
27335.e: In the wet ground on lake shores there is no oxygen. That is why wood and textiles break down much more slowly there.

27336.q: What is the fabric woven from flax fibres called?
27336.e: Linen is woven from flax yarn. In the lake-dwelling settlements, linen was the most important woven fabric.

27337.q: How were the lintel stones of Stonehenge fixed onto the standing stones?
a: With pegs and holes as in wooden buildings
27337.e: Pegs are carved on top of the standing stones and fit into holes in the lintels. This kind of joint is otherwise known from woodwork.
27337.m: The stones of Stonehenge are joined like pieces of wood.

27340.q: What is a “henge”, after which Stonehenge is named?
a: A round earth bank with a ditch
27340.e: A henge is a circular site made of an earth bank and a ditch. Stonehenge began as such a site before the stones arrived.
27340.m: A henge is a circle of bank and ditch.

27341.q: What is particularly amazing about the stones of Stonehenge?
a: Some came from hundreds of kilometres away
27341.e: Some stones come from Wales and one even from Scotland. People moved them over long distances without machines.
27341.m: Some of the stones of Stonehenge came from far away.

27342.q: Roughly what is the diameter of the outer stone circle of Stonehenge?
27342.e: The circle of sarsen stones measures about 33 metres across. The whole site with bank and ditch is much larger.
27342.m: The stone circle of Stonehenge measures just over 30 metres.

27344.q: How long was the Grand Menhir Brisé in Brittany, the largest known menhir in Europe?
27344.e: The menhir near Locmariaquer is now broken into four pieces. Together they are about 20 metres long and weigh several hundred tonnes.
27344.m: The largest menhir in Europe was about 20 metres long.

27345.q: Which famous monument in England is a circle of huge standing stones?
27345.e: Stonehenge was begun around 5000 years ago. Stone circles like this also exist in Brittany.
27345.m: Stonehenge is a famous stone circle.

27346.q: What are the large stone tombs of the New Stone Age in northern Germany often called?
27346.e: People used to believe that only giants, called “Hünen” in German, could have moved such big stones. That is where the name Hünengrab comes from.
27346.m: Large stone tombs in northern Germany are called giants' graves.

a: A burial chamber reached by a long passage
A grave in the middle of a road
A grave inside a tree trunk
27347.e: In a passage grave, a passage made of stone slabs leads into the chamber. The whole thing is usually covered by an earth mound.
27347.m: A passage of stones leads to a passage grave.

27348.q: What happens in the Irish passage grave of Newgrange on the days around the winter solstice?
a: Sunlight shines all the way into the burial chamber
27348.e: Above the entrance there is an opening for light. At sunrise the light then shines through the long passage into the chamber.
27348.m: At Newgrange the winter sun shines into the burial chamber.

27349.q: In which country is the huge Dolmen de Menga?
27349.e: The Dolmen de Menga is near Antequera in Andalusia. It is one of the largest megalithic tombs in Europe and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
27349.m: The Dolmen de Menga is in Spain.

27350.q: How was the Le Petit-Chasseur necropolis discovered in 1961?
a: From aerial photos taken from a plane
27350.e: While building blocks of flats, workers came across large stone slabs. After that, archaeological excavations began.
27350.m: Le Petit-Chasseur was discovered on a building site in 1961.

27351.e: Necropolis comes from Greek: “nekros” means dead and “polis” means city. It refers to a large burial ground.
27351.m: A necropolis is a city of the dead.

27352.q: What do the engraved stone stelae of Le Petit-Chasseur show?
a: Human figures with weapons and clothing
27352.e: The stelae show very simplified people. Engraved on them are, for example, belts, decorated clothes and weapons.
27352.m: The stelae of Sion show people.

27353.q: In which town in Valais is the Le Petit-Chasseur necropolis?
27353.e: The graves lie in a residential area of Sion. They are among the most important New Stone Age sites in Switzerland.
27353.m: The Le Petit-Chasseur necropolis is in Sion.

27354.q: From which period do the graves of Le Petit-Chasseur mainly date?
a: From the end of the New Stone Age and the Copper Age
From the Ice Age 30,000 years ago
27354.e: The site was used from about 2900 to 2200 BC. Later, people of the Bell Beaker culture also buried their dead there.
27354.m: Le Petit-Chasseur dates from the third millennium BC.

27355.q: What is a stele, like the ones found at Le Petit-Chasseur?
a: An upright stone with pictures or signs
27355.e: Stelae are stone slabs set upright. In Sion, human figures with belts, clothes and weapons were engraved on them.
27355.m: A stele is a stone with engraved pictures.

27356.q: Which weapon is typically shown on the older stelae of Le Petit-Chasseur?
27356.e: The older stelae show belts with a dagger. The younger stelae, on the other hand, show bows and arrows.
27356.m: Older stelae in Sion show daggers.

27357.q: Roughly how many engraved stelae were found in the excavations from 1961 onwards?
27357.e: More than 30 decorated stone stelae came to light in the necropolis. Many had later been broken and used as building material for graves.
27357.m: Over 30 stelae were found in Sion.

27358.q: Between which two ages does the Copper Age lie?
a: Between the New Stone Age and the Bronze Age
Between the Bronze Age and the Iron Age
Between the Iron Age and Roman times
Between the Old Stone Age and the Middle Stone Age
27358.e: At the end of the New Stone Age, people began to work copper. Later they mixed copper with tin, and the Bronze Age began.
27358.m: The Copper Age lies between the New Stone Age and the Bronze Age.

27359.q: Why did people in the Copper Age still use many stone tools?
a: Copper was only known from books
27359.e: Copper had to be extracted from ore with great effort and was valuable. That is why stone tools stayed in everyday use for a long time.
27359.m: In the Copper Age people used copper and stone side by side.

27360.q: Where was Ötzi, a man from the Copper Age, found in 1991?
a: In the ice of a glacier in the Alps
In the desert sand in Egypt
27360.e: Hikers found Ötzi in the Ötztal Alps on the border between Italy and Austria. The ice had preserved him for over 5000 years.
27360.m: Ötzi lay in the glacier ice of the Alps for over 5000 years.

27361.q: What do you have to do with copper ore to get pure copper from it?
a: Heat it strongly in a fire
Grind it to powder and eat it
27361.e: In smelting, the ore is heated very strongly with charcoal. This separates the metal from the rock.
27361.m: Copper is obtained by heating ore.

27362.q: Which precious metal did people in the Copper Age also already make into jewellery?
27362.e: Gold is often found pure in nature and is easy to shape. Lots of gold jewellery was found in Copper Age graves, for example in Varna in Bulgaria.
27362.m: There was already gold jewellery in the Copper Age.

27363.q: Which finds from the Pfyn culture in eastern Switzerland show that copper was worked there?
27363.e: Crucibles with remains of copper were found in Pfyn culture settlements. The metal was melted and cast in them.
27363.m: The Pfyn culture melted copper in crucibles.

27364.q: Why did copper not yet completely replace stone tools in the Copper Age?
27364.e: Tools made of pure copper quickly become blunt. Only the harder bronze largely replaced stone.
27364.m: Pure copper is rather soft for tools.

27365.q: Which green mineral is an important copper ore?
27365.e: Malachite is a bright green copper mineral. People probably discovered copper through eye-catching stones like this.
27365.m: Malachite is a green copper ore.

27366.q: In which region of Europe were some of the oldest traces of copper smelting found, around 7000 years old?
27366.e: In Belovode in present-day Serbia, slag from around 5000 BC was found. It shows that copper was extracted from ore there very early.
27366.m: Copper was smelted very early in the Balkans.

27367.q: What is done to flax stems during what is called retting?
a: They are left to rot partly in dew or water
They are roasted over the fire
27367.e: During retting, bacteria and fungi partly break down the stem. Afterwards the fibres come away from the woody part more easily.

27368.q: What do you do when you spin?
a: You twist fibres into a thread
27368.e: In spinning, short fibres such as flax or wool are twisted together. This makes a long, strong thread. Cloth is then woven from threads.
27368.m: Spinning turns fibres into a thread.

27369.q: Since when have people used plant fibres such as flax?
27369.e: Flax fibres over 30,000 years old were found in a cave. So people used fibres long before farming.
27369.m: People used flax fibres over 30,000 years ago.

27370.q: At roughly what altitude was the place where Ötzi was found?
27370.e: Ötzi lay in a rocky hollow at the Tisenjoch at about 3210 metres. There he was covered by ice for over 5000 years.
27370.m: Ötzi lay at an altitude of over 3000 metres.

27371.q: On the territory of which present-day country was Ötzi found?
27371.e: The site is in South Tyrol, only about 90 metres from the border with Austria. New measurements showed that it is on Italian territory.
27371.m: Ötzi was found in South Tyrol.

27372.q: Which weapons did Ötzi carry with him?
a: A bow and arrows and a copper axe
27372.e: Ötzi had a bow, a quiver of arrows, a flint dagger and an axe with a copper blade with him.
27372.m: Ötzi carried a bow and arrows and a copper axe.

27373.q: What was Ötzi's small wooden tool with an antler tip used for?
27373.e: With this retouching tool, Ötzi pressed small chips off flint blades. That kept his tools sharp.
27373.m: Ötzi could resharpen his flint blades himself.

27374.q: What did a DNA study from 2023 show about Ötzi's appearance?
a: He had rather dark skin and hardly any hair on his head
He had blond curls and blue eyes
He had red hair and freckles
He was over two metres tall
27374.e: The study showed that Ötzi had darker skin than previously thought and was probably bald. His ancestors came mainly from early farmers from Anatolia.
27374.m: Ötzi probably had dark skin and was bald.

27375.q: According to his DNA, which food intolerance did Ötzi have?
a: He could not digest milk well
27375.e: The analysis of his DNA showed lactose intolerance. At that time, adults usually could not yet digest milk.

27376.q: Who gave the glacier mummy the nickname “Ötzi”?
27376.e: The Viennese journalist Karl Wendl came up with the name shortly after the find. It quickly became known all over the world.
27376.m: A journalist came up with the name Ötzi.

27377.q: Why was Ötzi so well preserved?
a: He lay in glacier ice for thousands of years
He was embalmed like a mummy in Egypt
He lay in a golden coffin
27377.e: Ötzi lay in a rocky hollow over which the glacier flowed. Cold and ice protected his body from decaying.
27377.m: The glacier ice preserved Ötzi for over 5000 years.

27379.q: According to the usual interpretation, what do the two golden arcs on the edge of the Nebra sky disc show?
a: The path of sunrises and sunsets over the year
27379.e: Each arc covers about 82 degrees. At the place where it was found, this matches the stretch of horizon where the sun rises and sets between the start of summer and the start of winter.
27379.m: The edge arcs of the sky disc show the path of the sun on the horizon.

27380.q: In which Swiss city did the police recover the Nebra sky disc in 2002?
27380.e: The dealers in stolen goods wanted to sell the disc in a hotel in Basel. An archaeologist pretended to be a buyer, and the Swiss police moved in.
27380.m: The sky disc was recovered in Basel in 2002.

27381.q: Apart from its gold inlays, what metal is the Nebra sky disc made of?
27381.e: The disc was cast and hammered from bronze. The sun, moon and stars are made of gold sheet laid on top.
27381.m: The sky disc is a bronze disc with gold inlays.

27382.q: Which star cluster do many researchers see in the group of seven gold dots on the Nebra sky disc?
27382.e: The seven dots lying close together are usually interpreted as the Pleiades. This star cluster was important for farmers' calendars.
27382.m: The seven gold dots probably represent the Pleiades.

27383.q: Roughly how old is the Nebra sky disc?
27383.e: The disc dates from the Bronze Age. It was made and buried around 3600 years ago.
27383.m: The sky disc is about 3600 years old.

27384.q: In which country was the Nebra sky disc found?
27384.e: Treasure hunters found the disc in 1999 near Nebra in Saxony-Anhalt. Today it is in the museum in Halle.
27384.m: The sky disc comes from Germany.

27385.q: Which natural resource was already being mined in Hallstatt over 3000 years ago?
27385.e: People were already mining salt in the mountain above Hallstatt in prehistoric times. Salt was valuable because it could be used to preserve meat.
27385.m: Salt was mined in Hallstatt in prehistoric times.

27386.q: Which period begins in Central Europe with the later Hallstatt period around 800 BC?
27386.e: From about 800 BC, tools and weapons made of iron became widespread. That is why it is called the early Iron Age.
27386.m: In our region the Iron Age begins with the Hallstatt period.

27387.q: In which country is Hallstatt, after which a prehistoric period is named?
27387.e: Hallstatt is in Austria. Because of the many rich finds there, the early Iron Age is called the Hallstatt period.
27387.m: The Hallstatt period is named after a place in Austria.

27388.q: How were the dead buried in the Hallstatt cemetery?
27388.e: About half of the dead were buried unburnt, the others were cremated. Both kinds of burial existed side by side.
27388.m: Hallstatt had both body burials and cremation burials.

27389.q: Where did the powerful families of the Hallstatt period often live?
a: In caves deep inside the mountain
In pile dwellings in the middle of a lake
27389.e: The powerful lived on fortified hills and traded as far as the Mediterranean. Experts call these places princely seats.
27389.m: The powerful people of the Hallstatt period lived on fortified hills.

27390.q: Why were prehistoric clothes and tools well preserved in the Hallstatt salt mine?
27390.e: Salt draws water out of bacteria and so prevents rotting. That is why even scraps of cloth and wooden shovels were found in the mine.

27391.q: For roughly how many years have people been getting salt in Hallstatt?
27391.e: The oldest traces of salt use go back to the New Stone Age. That is why Hallstatt is considered one of the oldest salt mines in the world.
27391.m: Salt has been mined in Hallstatt for about 7000 years.

27392.q: How did people get salt in Hallstatt in prehistoric times?
a: They dug tunnels deep into the mountain
They collected it from the surface
They fished it out of the river
27392.e: In Hallstatt the salt lies in the rock of the mountain. The miners dug long tunnels and knocked the salt out with picks.
27392.m: In Hallstatt salt was mined in tunnels inside the mountain.

27393.q: From which period does the famous wooden staircase from the Hallstatt salt mountain date?
27393.e: The tree rings in the wood show that the trees were cut down over 3300 years ago. So the staircase dates from the Bronze Age.
27393.m: The Hallstatt wooden staircase dates from the Bronze Age.

27394.q: Why were wood, leather and cloth so well preserved in the Hallstatt salt mine?
27394.e: Salt draws out water and slows down bacteria and fungi. That is why even scraps of clothing and carrying sacks did not rot.
27394.m: Salt is a natural protection against rotting.

27395.q: What did people in prehistoric times mainly need salt for?
27395.e: Without a fridge, meat and fish could only be kept with salt, smoke or drying. That made salt a valuable trading good.
27395.m: People used salt to make food last.

27396.q: What did miners discover in the Hallstatt salt mountain in 1734?
a: A dead body preserved in salt
27396.e: The so-called “Man in Salt” was a prehistoric miner who had died in an accident. He was buried in the Hallstatt churchyard at the time.
27396.m: The “Man in Salt” was found in 1734.

27397.q: What did prehistoric miners use to light the tunnels in Hallstatt?
27397.e: Countless burnt wooden splints were found in the mine. They were tied into bundles and lit.
27397.m: Wooden splints gave the miners light.

27398.q: What material did the Celts of the La Tène period use to make colourful, seamless bracelets?
27398.e: The rings were drawn from hot glass and often coloured blue, brown or yellow. They were popular jewellery for women.
27398.m: Celtic women wore colourful glass bracelets.

27399.q: Which people is the La Tène culture linked with?
27399.e: Greek and Roman writers called the peoples north of the Alps Celts or Gauls. Their culture largely matches the La Tène finds.
27399.m: The La Tène culture is the culture of the Celts.

27400.q: What do the pictures on the famous Gundestrup cauldron show?
27400.e: The silver cauldron is richly decorated. Its pictures show gods, warriors and animals in the Celtic style.
27400.m: The Gundestrup cauldron shows Celtic gods and warriors.

27401.q: What is the later Iron Age, the La Tène period, named after?
27401.e: Because so many typical finds lay at La Tène, the whole period was named after this place. The name caught on across Europe.
27401.m: The La Tène period is named after a site in Switzerland.

27402.q: What is the pin called that the Celts used to fasten their clothes?
27402.e: The fibula works much like a safety pin. Because its shape often changed, fibulae help to date finds.
27402.m: A fibula is a brooch for clothing.

27403.q: What does the Celtic god Cernunnos wear on his head in many pictures?
27403.e: Cernunnos usually sits cross-legged, surrounded by animals. He is seen as the god of nature and animals.
27403.m: Cernunnos is the Celtic god with deer antlers.

27404.q: Which device for grinding grain spread during the La Tène period?
27404.e: With a rotary quern you turn an upper stone on a lower one. This was much faster than rubbing on a flat grinding stone.
27404.m: The Celts ground their grain with the rotary quern.

27405.q: Which canton is the La Tène site in?
27405.e: The site is near Marin-Epagnier, now in the municipality of La Tène. The finds can be seen in the cantonal museum.
27405.m: The La Tène site is in the canton of Neuchâtel.

27406.q: Who pulled the first weapons out of the water at La Tène in 1857?
27406.e: A fisherman, working for the collector Friedrich Schwab from Biel, brought weapons up from the shallow water. That was how research at the site began.
27406.m: A fisherman recovered the first finds from La Tène.

27407.q: Why did many finds come to light at La Tène from around 1870?
a: The water level of the lake was lowered
An earthquake opened up the ground
27407.e: During the Jura water correction, the level of Lake Neuchâtel was lowered. As a result, many sites on the shore were suddenly dry.
27407.m: The Jura water correction brought many finds to light at La Tène.

27408.q: Which river flows out of Lake Neuchâtel at the La Tène site?
27408.e: The Thielle connects Lake Neuchâtel with Lake Biel. Its course was later straightened.
27408.m: At La Tène the Thielle flows out of Lake Neuchâtel.

27409.q: What is the municipality of La Tène on Lake Neuchâtel named after?
27409.e: When municipalities merged in 2009, the new municipality chose the name of the site. In this way it remembers its Celtic past.
27409.m: The municipality of La Tène bears the name of the site.

27410.q: What else was found at La Tène besides weapons and tools?
27410.e: Whether the dead were sacrificed, died in battle or were killed in an accident is still unclear. How to interpret the site remains disputed.
27410.m: Human skeletons were also found at La Tène.

27411.q: What does the Latin word “oppidum” generally mean?
27411.e: The Romans used it for smaller towns and fortified places. Archaeologists now use it for the Celtic centres.
27411.m: The Latin word oppidum means town.

27412.q: Which Roman general used the word “oppidum” for Celtic towns in his account of the Gallic War?
27412.e: In his work “De bello Gallico”, Caesar described many Gallic places as oppida. That is where today's technical term comes from.
27412.m: We know the term oppidum from Caesar's war account.

27413.q: What did the Celts build the walls of their oppida from?
27413.e: The wall was called murus gallicus, the Gallic wall. A frame of wooden beams with long iron nails was filled with earth and faced with stones.
27413.m: Celtic walls were made of wood, earth and stone.

27414.e: Oppida were large Celtic settlements protected by walls. People traded, lived and worked there.
27414.m: An oppidum was a fortified Celtic settlement.

27415.q: On which hill in the old town of Basel was there a Celtic oppidum?
27415.e: The Münsterhügel (Cathedral Hill) rises above the Rhine and was easy to defend. The Celts protected it with a rampart and a ditch.
27415.m: There was a Celtic oppidum on Basel's Münsterhügel.

27416.q: According to Caesar, why did the Helvetii burn their own oppida before leaving in 58 BC?
a: So that nobody would think of returning
So that the Romans would not see them
Because a plague had broken out
Because they were celebrating a festival
27416.e: Caesar reports that the Helvetii burned twelve oppida and around 400 villages. In this way they wanted to make any return impossible.
27416.m: The Helvetii burned their settlements before leaving.

27417.e: Bibracte was the main town of the Aedui and lay on Mont Beuvray. Today there is a large museum of Celtic culture there.
27417.m: Bibracte was an important Celtic oppidum.

27418.q: Between which two lakes does Mont Vully rise?
27418.e: Mont Vully is a hill in the Three Lakes region. From the top you can see two lakes and the Alps.
27418.m: Mont Vully lies between Lake Murten and Lake Neuchâtel.

27419.q: Which Celtic people lived in the oppidum on Mont Vully?
27419.e: In the 1st century BC, the Swiss Plateau was the territory of the Helvetii. Mont Vully was one of their fortified main centres.
27419.m: The Helvetii lived on Mont Vully.

27420.q: What is the southern slope of Mont Vully known for today?
27420.e: The sunny slopes above Lake Murten are well suited to vines. The wine from the area is called Vully.

27421.q: For which event was a section of the Celtic wall on Mont Vully rebuilt?
27421.e: The 2002 national exhibition took place partly in Murten. The reconstruction shows what the Celtic fortification looked like.
27421.m: The wall reconstruction on Mont Vully was built for Expo.02.

27422.q: Roughly how long was the defensive rampart of the oppidum on Mont Vully?
27422.e: The rampart closed off the hill on the side that could be reached. The other sides were protected by steep slopes.
27422.m: The rampart on Mont Vully was about 600 metres long.

27423.q: Which canton is the oppidum on Mont Vully in?
27423.e: The hill is in the Lake district near Murten. The region is bilingual, German and French.
27423.m: The oppidum on Mont Vully is in the canton of Fribourg.

27424.q: According to a Roman account, what did the druids use to cut mistletoe from the oak?
27424.e: The Roman Pliny the Elder describes the mistletoe ritual. A druid in a white robe cut the mistletoe with a golden sickle.
27424.m: The druids cut mistletoe with a golden sickle.

27425.q: How do we know a lot about the druids today?
a: From reports by Romans such as Caesar
27425.e: The druids passed on their knowledge by word of mouth. What we know comes mainly from Greek and Roman writers, who wrote from their own point of view.
27425.m: It is mainly Roman writers who tell us about the druids.

27426.e: There were druids among the Celts in Gaul and Britain. They were priests, judges and teachers.

27427.q: According to Caesar, how many chief druids stood at the head of all druids?
27427.e: When this leader died, the most respected druid took over. If there were several equally strong candidates, there was a vote or even a fight.
27427.m: According to Caesar, the druids had a single leader.

27428.q: According to Caesar, what did the druids teach about the soul?
a: It does not die but passes into another body
It disappears for ever at death
It lives on in the gravestone
27428.e: Caesar thought this belief took away the warriors' fear of death. This is called the transmigration of souls.
27428.m: The druids believed in the transmigration of souls.

27429.q: According to Caesar, why did the Gallic druids gather once a year at a sacred place?
a: To judge cases and settle disputes
To choose a king for Rome
27429.e: The meeting took place in the territory of the Carnutes, which was seen as the centre of Gaul. Anyone with a dispute came there and let the druids decide.
27429.m: The druids judged cases at their yearly meeting.

27430.q: How did the Romans treat the druids?
a: They fought them and banned their cult
They built temples for them in Rome
They let them lead the army
27430.e: The Romans saw the druids as a threat to their rule. They banned the cult and around AD 60 even attacked their centre on an island off Wales.
27430.m: The Romans fought against the druids.

27431.q: What did the Celts need coins for?
27431.e: With coins the Celts could buy and sell goods more easily. They also traded with the Romans.
27431.m: The Celts used coins for trade.

27432.q: What are the curved Celtic gold coins called that are linked to legends about the rainbow?
27432.e: After heavy rain, such coins sometimes turned up in fields. People believed they had fallen down at the end of the rainbow.
27432.m: Rainbow cups are curved Celtic gold coins.

27433.q: Which metals make up the alloy potin, from which many Celtic coins were made?
27433.e: Potin contains a lot of tin, which makes it easy to cast. Such coins were small change for everyday use.
27433.m: Potin is an alloy of copper, tin and lead.

27434.q: In which Swiss city were large lumps of melted-together Celtic coins found in 1890?
27434.e: The lumps came to light near today's Alpenquai in Zurich. The largest weighs almost 60 kilograms.
27434.m: Lumps of Celtic coins were found in Zurich.

27435.q: What is the large potin lump from Zurich made of?
27435.e: Thousands of coins melted together in a fire. They were probably laid down as an offering.
27435.m: The Zurich potin lump is made of thousands of coins.

27436.q: Which animal is shown on the back of many Celtic coins?
27436.e: The design goes back to Greek models showing a chariot team. The Celts often showed it in a very simplified and strange way.
27436.m: Many Celtic coins show a horse.

27437.q: In which place in Baden-Württemberg was the unrobbed grave of a Celtic prince discovered in 1977?
27437.e: The grave had been spared by grave robbers. That is why the grave goods were found almost complete, including gold jewellery and a large bronze cauldron.
27437.m: The famous grave of a Celtic prince is in Hochdorf.

27438.q: What was the hat found in the prince's grave at Hochdorf made of?
27438.e: The cone-shaped hat was finely decorated. A stone figure from the Hallstatt period wears a similar hat.
27438.m: The prince of Hochdorf wore a hat made of birch bark.

27439.q: What is another technical name for a burial mound?
27439.e: The word comes from Latin and means “mound”. A menhir, on the other hand, is a single standing stone.
27439.m: A tumulus is a burial mound.

27440.q: Why are many Iron Age burial mounds well preserved today, especially in forests?
a: The ground there was not ploughed
There were never grave robbers there
27440.e: On farmland the mounds were ploughed flat over the centuries. In the forest they stayed visible as bumps.
27440.m: Many burial mounds have survived in forests.

27441.q: Which vehicle did people of the Hallstatt period often put in the graves of rich people?
27441.e: The wagon showed the high rank of the dead person. Often there were also horse harness and drinking vessels.
27441.m: Hallstatt princes were buried with wagons.

27442.q: What do especially richly furnished burial mounds show about Iron Age society?
a: That there was a powerful upper class
27442.e: Only a few dead people were given gold, wagons and goods imported from the south. Most graves were much simpler.
27442.m: Rich graves are evidence of an upper class.

27443.q: What did Iron Age people pile up over the grave of an important person?
a: A mound of earth and stones
A layer of sand from the sea
27443.e: A mound of earth and stones was built over the burial chamber. Some burial mounds can still be seen in forests today.
27443.m: Burial mounds are heaps piled up over graves.

27444.q: In which area did the Celtic people called the Rauraci live?
a: At the Rhine bend around Basel
27444.e: The Rauraci settled on the Upper Rhine and in the Jura. Several of their settlements lie in what is now the city of Basel.
27444.m: The Rauraci lived in the Basel area.

27445.q: With which people did the Rauraci set off for Gaul in 58 BC?
27445.e: After their defeat by Caesar at Bibracte, the emigrants had to return to their homeland.
27445.m: The Rauraci left together with the Helvetii.

27446.q: Which Roman town bears the name of the Rauraci?
27446.e: The town is near Augst and Kaiseraugst on the Rhine. It is one of the best-preserved Roman towns north of the Alps.
27446.m: Augusta Raurica is named after the Rauraci.

27447.q: Which people founded a colony in the territory of the Rauraci?
27447.e: The Romans founded a colony in the territory of the Rauraci. It later became the town of Augusta Raurica near Augst.
27447.m: The Romans founded a colony in the territory of the Rauraci.

27448.q: What was discovered in 1911 while a gasworks was being built in Basel?
27448.e: During building work, remains of a large Celtic settlement were found. It was an important centre of trade and crafts for the Rauraci.
27448.m: Remains of a large Rauraci settlement were found in Basel.

27449.q: Which group of peoples did the Rauraci belong to?
27449.e: The Rauraci were a Celtic tribe. Like the Helvetii, they lived in the area of present-day Switzerland before the Romans arrived.

27450.e: Vercingetorix was a chieftain of the Arverni in Gaul. He led many Gallic tribes in the fight against Rome.
27450.m: Vercingetorix was a leader of the Gauls.

27451.e: Julius Caesar wanted to conquer all of Gaul. Vercingetorix led the last great uprising of the Gauls against him.

27452.q: At which town did Vercingetorix have to surrender to Caesar?
27452.e: Caesar trapped Vercingetorix in Alesia behind huge earthworks. When supplies ran out, the Gaul had to surrender.

27453.q: In which present-day country was most of Gaul?
27453.e: Gaul mainly covered present-day France, as well as Belgium and parts of Switzerland. Many Celtic tribes lived there.
27453.m: Gaul was mainly in present-day France.

27454.q: What happened to Vercingetorix after he surrendered?
a: He was taken to Rome and later executed
He fell in the last battle
27454.e: He was held prisoner for several years and paraded in Caesar's triumph. After that he was killed.
27454.m: Vercingetorix died as a prisoner in Rome.

27455.q: How is Vercingetorix seen in France today?
27455.e: In the 19th century Vercingetorix became a hero in France. He stands for the brave fight for freedom.
27455.m: Vercingetorix is a national hero of France.

27456.q: Which tactic did Vercingetorix use to weaken the Romans?
a: He had villages and supplies burned
He dug tunnels under the camps
27456.e: The Romans were not supposed to find any grain or fodder in Gaul. This way of waging war is called a scorched-earth tactic.

27457.q: What does dendrochronology examine in order to date wood?
27457.e: The word comes from the Greek “dendron” for tree. Each ring stands for one year of growth.
27457.m: Dendrochronology dates wood using tree rings.

27458.q: How many tree rings does a tree in Central Europe normally form each year?
27458.e: In spring, light, loose wood grows, and in late summer darker, denser wood. Together they make one ring.
27458.m: In our region a tree forms one ring every year.

27459.q: Why are tree rings not all the same width?
a: The weather affects growth every year
The bark presses with different force
The roots only grow every two years
27459.e: In warm, damp years a tree grows more than in cold or dry ones. This creates a typical pattern of wide and narrow rings.
27459.m: The weather decides how wide the tree rings are.

27460.q: What do archaeologists use the tree rings of wooden posts from lake-dwelling settlements for?
a: To find the year of felling almost exactly
To find out the colour of the houses
To see how many people lived there
To calculate the weight of the houses
27460.e: The pattern of wide and narrow rings is compared with a tree-ring calendar. This often shows exactly in which year a tree was cut down.
27460.m: Tree rings can date wood very precisely.

27461.q: Which tool is used to take a tree-ring sample from a living tree without cutting it down?
27461.e: The hollow tool pulls out a thin stick of wood from the middle of the trunk. The tree survives this small operation.
27461.m: Tree-ring samples are taken with an increment borer.

27462.q: How can tree rings reach back thousands of years into the past?
a: Ring patterns of living trees are linked with old wood
The rings of one very old tree are counted
The thickness of the bark is measured
New trees are planted and people wait
27462.e: The ring patterns of living trees, old beams and wood from the ground overlap. This creates a long, unbroken sequence.
27462.m: Overlapping ring patterns make a long tree-ring calendar.

27463.q: What can be worked out if the last ring under the bark has survived on a piece of wood?
a: The exact year the tree was felled
27463.e: This outermost ring is called the waney edge. If it is missing, only the earliest possible year of felling can be given.
27463.m: With the waney edge, the year of felling can be worked out exactly.

27465.q: Up to roughly what age can finds be dated with the radiocarbon method?
27465.e: After around 50,000 years, almost all the measurable carbon has decayed. Older finds need other methods.
27465.m: The radiocarbon method reaches back about 50,000 years.

27466.q: Why can dinosaur bones not be dated with the radiocarbon method?
27466.e: The method only works up to about 50,000 years. But dinosaurs lived over 66 million years ago.
27466.m: The radiocarbon method is no good for very old fossils.

27467.q: What do researchers find out with the radiocarbon method?
a: Which country a find comes from
How much a find is worth
27467.e: Plants, animals and humans contain carbon-14. After death it slowly decays. The age is calculated from what is left.
27467.m: The radiocarbon method is used to find the age of finds.

27468.q: What fraction of the original carbon-14 is left after two half-lives?
27468.e: After one half-life, half is left. After another half-life, this remainder halves again: 1/2 times 1/2 makes 1/4.
27468.m: With every half-life the amount halves.

27469.q: Which find can be dated with the radiocarbon method?
27469.e: Only material that comes from living things and contains carbon can be dated. This includes wood, bones, seeds and textiles.
27469.m: The radiocarbon method only works on organic material.

27470.q: Up to roughly what age can the radiocarbon method be used?
27470.e: In older samples there is almost no carbon-14 left. The tiny remains can then no longer be measured reliably.
27470.m: The radiocarbon method reaches back about 50,000 years.

27471.q: In an undisturbed deposit, which layer is usually the oldest?
27471.e: New layers are always laid down on top of existing ones. So whatever lies deeper was there first.

a: The order of layers of earth and rock
27472.e: Stratigraphy is the study of layers. It shows which layer formed first and which formed later.
27472.m: Stratigraphy is the study of layers.

27473.q: How do many layers of earth and rock form?
a: Material builds up bit by bit
They grow out of the ground like plants
27473.e: Sand, mud, ash or rubbish build up on top of each other over a long time. This is how layer after layer forms.
27473.m: Layers form when material builds up bit by bit.

27474.q: Above a layer with stone tools there is a layer with Roman pottery fragments. What follows from this?
27474.e: In an undisturbed deposit, older layers lie at the bottom. So the stone tools were laid down earlier than the fragments.
27474.m: Whatever lies underneath is usually older.

27475.q: What kind of dating does stratigraphy alone provide?
a: A date accurate to the day
27475.e: The order of layers only says what is older or younger. For actual years, extra methods are needed.
27475.m: Stratigraphy shows what is older and what is younger.

27476.q: What can archaeologists see particularly well on the vertical wall of an excavation?
27476.e: On the vertical wall you can see the layers like in a cross-section. Archaeologists draw and photograph them carefully.
27476.m: You can see the layers on the excavation wall.

27477.q: Why do archaeologists record every layer with drawings, photos and measurements?
a: Because photos are worth more than finds
Because the layers would otherwise grow back
Because finds without photos are forbidden
27477.e: A layer that has been removed cannot be put back. Only careful records allow new studies later.
27477.m: Digging destroys layers, so everything must be recorded carefully.

27478.q: Which city did King Hammurabi rule over?
27478.e: Hammurabi (also Hammurapi) was king of Babylon. He made the city the centre of a large empire in Mesopotamia.
27478.m: Hammurabi was a powerful king of Babylon.

27479.q: In which script is the Code of Hammurabi written?
27479.e: In Mesopotamia people wrote with wedge-shaped signs. Hammurabi’s laws are also carved into the stone in cuneiform.
27479.m: The Code of Hammurabi is written in cuneiform.

27480.q: What did Hammurabi have his laws written on so that everyone could see them?
27480.e: The laws are on a stele over two metres high made of hard, dark stone. That way they were preserved for a long time.
27480.m: Hammurabi’s laws are on a stone pillar.

27481.q: What does the old rule “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” mean?
a: The punishment should match the harm
You should forgive everyone at once
Punishments are only paid in money
27481.e: Anyone who harmed someone was to suffer something equal. This principle is called the law of retaliation.
27481.m: “An eye for an eye” means the punishment matches the harm.

27482.q: According to the preface of his laws, whom did Hammurabi want to protect?
27482.e: In the prologue Hammurabi writes that he was to bring justice so that the strong would not harm the weak. In this way he presents himself as a just shepherd of his people.
27482.m: Hammurabi’s laws were meant to protect the weak from the strong.

27483.q: What did the size of a punishment in the Code of Hammurabi often depend on?
a: The social rank of offender and victim
The weather on the day of the crime
27483.e: Society was divided into free people, semi-free people and slaves. Anyone who injured a free person was usually punished more harshly than for injuring a slave.
27483.m: In the Code of Hammurabi the punishment often depended on the rank of those involved.

27484.q: In which present-day country was Hammurabi’s law stele rediscovered in 1901?
27484.e: An Elamite king had taken the stele to the city of Susa as war booty. There, in present-day Iran, French archaeologists found it again.
27484.m: Hammurabi’s stele was found in present-day Iran.

27485.q: According to the Code of Hammurabi, what punishment did a builder face if a house he built collapsed and killed the owner?
27485.e: The Code states that in this case the builder is to be put to death. The harsh rule was meant to make sure buildings were built carefully.
27485.m: The Code of Hammurabi punished bad builders very harshly.

27486.q: According to the epic, how much of Gilgamesh is divine?
27486.e: The epic describes Gilgamesh as two thirds god and one third human. His mother was the goddess Ninsun.
27486.m: According to the epic, Gilgamesh is two thirds divine.

27487.q: In which region is the Epic of Gilgamesh set?
27487.e: Gilgamesh was king of Uruk in southern Mesopotamia, in present-day Iraq. The oldest stories about him were written down in Sumerian.
27487.m: The Epic of Gilgamesh comes from Mesopotamia.

27488.q: Which goddess does Gilgamesh turn down when she wants to marry him?
27488.e: Gilgamesh lists how badly things went for her earlier lovers. Offended, the goddess then sends a monster against him.
27488.m: In the epic Gilgamesh rejects the goddess Ishtar.

27489.q: Which story from the Bible is the flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh similar to?
27489.e: In the Epic of Gilgamesh, too, a man builds a boat and survives a great flood. In 1872 a researcher recognised this similarity on a clay tablet.
27489.m: The flood in the Epic of Gilgamesh is similar to the story of Noah.

27490.q: What is the Epic of Gilgamesh?
a: One of the oldest hero stories
27490.e: The Epic of Gilgamesh tells of King Gilgamesh and his search for immortality. The best-known version is on twelve clay tablets.
27490.m: The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest hero stories in the world.

27491.q: Roughly how old is the Epic of Gilgamesh?
27491.e: The first Gilgamesh stories were created about 4000 years ago. The best-known tablets come from the library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal in the 7th century BC.
27491.m: The Epic of Gilgamesh is several thousand years old.

27492.q: Which test does Gilgamesh fail at the home of the flood survivor?
27492.e: Gilgamesh is meant to show that he can conquer sleep. But he falls asleep at once and so proves that he cannot become immortal.
27492.m: Gilgamesh fails the test of staying awake.

27493.q: At the end of the epic, what does Gilgamesh proudly show on his return?
27493.e: At the end Gilgamesh takes his companion up onto the mighty wall of his city. His building thus becomes what remains of him.
27493.m: At the end of the epic Gilgamesh proudly shows the wall of his city.

27494.e: A ziggurat is a large tower made of several steps, with a shrine at the top. There were such buildings in many cities of Mesopotamia.
27494.m: A ziggurat is a stepped temple tower in Mesopotamia.

27495.q: Roughly how old is the Ziggurat of Ur?
27495.e: King Ur-Nammu had the ziggurat built around 2100 BC. That is about 4100 years ago.
27495.m: The Ziggurat of Ur is about 4000 years old.

27496.q: What happened to the Ziggurat of Ur about 1500 years after it was built?
a: A Babylonian king had it restored
It was turned into a church
It was excavated for the first time
27496.e: In the 6th century BC the Babylonian king Nabonidus had old shrines restored. These included the Ziggurat of Ur.
27496.m: The Ziggurat of Ur was already restored in ancient times.

27497.q: What is the core of the Ziggurat of Ur made of?
27497.e: In Mesopotamia there was hardly any stone, but lots of mud. The core is made of sun-dried bricks, the outer shell of fired bricks with bitumen as mortar.
27497.m: The Ziggurat of Ur was built of mud bricks.

27498.q: How did people get up the Ziggurat of Ur?
27498.e: At the front three staircases lead up, one straight from the front and two at the sides along the wall. They meet at the top at a gatehouse.
27498.m: Stairs on the outside led up the ziggurat.

27499.q: What did archaeologists find at Ur next to the ziggurat in the 1920s?
27499.e: The British archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated Ur from 1922 to 1934. He found the ziggurat and tombs with gold, jewellery and musical instruments.
27499.m: Rich royal tombs were found at Ur.

27500.q: Which people made Ur one of their most important cities?
27500.e: Ur was one of the most important cities of the Sumerians in southern Mesopotamia. The Sumerians were one of the world’s first civilisations.
27500.m: Ur was an important city of the Sumerians.

27501.q: Which animals are shown on the bricks of the Ishtar Gate?
27501.e: Rows of bulls and dragons can be seen on the gate. They were sacred animals of the gods of Babylon.
27501.m: The Ishtar Gate shows bulls and dragons.

27502.q: In which city did the Ishtar Gate originally stand?
27502.e: The gate was one of the main gates in the city wall of Babylon. Through this gate you entered the inner city from the north.
27502.m: The Ishtar Gate was a city gate of Babylon.

27503.q: What was the goddess Ishtar, after whom the gate is named, responsible for?
27503.e: Ishtar was one of the most important goddesses of Mesopotamia. She was seen as the goddess of love, but also of war.
27503.m: Ishtar was the goddess of love and war.

27504.q: What is the main colour of the glazed bricks of the Ishtar Gate?
27504.e: The bricks are covered with a bright blue glaze. The yellow and brown animal figures stand out clearly against it.

27505.q: In which city is part of the Ishtar Gate in a museum today?
27505.e: German archaeologists took bricks from the gate to Berlin. In the Pergamon Museum the smaller front gate was rebuilt.
27505.m: The Ishtar Gate is now in Berlin.

27506.q: At which festival did the Babylonians march in a great procession through the Ishtar Gate?
27506.e: At the New Year festival, called Akitu, statues of the gods were carried through the gate in a solemn procession. The festival lasted several days in spring.
27506.m: At the New Year festival a procession passed through the Ishtar Gate.

27507.q: Roughly how old is the Ishtar Gate?
27507.e: The gate was built in Babylon around 575 BC. So it is about 2600 years old.
27507.m: The Ishtar Gate is about 2600 years old.

27508.q: On which river was the heartland of the Assyrians?
27508.e: The most important Assyrian cities lay on the upper Tigris in northern Mesopotamia. Today the area is part of northern Iraq.
27508.m: The heartland of the Assyrians was on the Tigris.

27509.q: What was the first capital of the Assyrians called, which has the same name as their chief god?
27509.e: The city of Assur was the religious centre of the Assyrians. The name of the people also comes from it and from the god of the same name.
27509.m: The city of Assur gave the Assyrians their name.

27510.q: Which huge stone figures guarded the gates of Assyrian palaces?
27510.e: The Assyrians called these guardian figures lamassu. They have the body of a bull or lion, wings and a bearded human head.
27510.m: Winged bulls with human heads guarded Assyrian gates.

27511.q: What did the Assyrians often do with conquered peoples to prevent uprisings?
a: They made them citizens of Assur.
They chose a new king for them.
27511.e: The Assyrians deported whole groups of people to other parts of their empire. People uprooted like this were meant to put up less resistance.
27511.m: The Assyrians often forcibly resettled conquered peoples.

27512.q: Which famous city on the Tigris was the Assyrian capital for a long time?
27512.e: Nineveh lay on the River Tigris in present-day Iraq. Under King Sennacherib it became the splendid capital of the Assyrian Empire.
27512.m: Nineveh was a great capital of the Assyrians.

27513.q: In which present-day country was the heartland of the Assyrians?
27513.e: The heartland of the Assyrians lay on the Tigris in the north of present-day Iraq. From there they conquered a large empire.
27513.m: The Assyrian Empire was centred in present-day Iraq.

27514.q: What did the Assyrian kings decorate the walls of their palaces with?
a: Stone reliefs of hunts and wars
27514.e: Large stone slabs with reliefs hung in the palaces. They showed the king hunting lions and his victories in war.
27514.m: Assyrian palaces were decorated with stone reliefs.

27515.q: Which country on the Nile did the Assyrians conquer in the 7th century BC?
27515.e: In 671 BC King Esarhaddon conquered Lower Egypt with the city of Memphis. With this, the Assyrian Empire reached its greatest size.
27515.m: In the 7th century BC the Assyrians even conquered Egypt.

27516.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Nineveh?
27516.e: Nineveh lies on the Tigris near the present-day city of Mosul in northern Iraq.
27516.m: The ruins of Nineveh are in Iraq.

27517.q: Which people made Nineveh their capital?
27517.e: Around 700 BC the Assyrian king Sennacherib built Nineveh up splendidly. It became one of the largest cities of its time.
27517.m: Nineveh was the capital of the Assyrians.

27518.q: What happened to the Assyrian Empire after Nineveh was destroyed?
27518.e: Nineveh fell in 612 BC after a long siege. After that the Assyrian Empire collapsed within a few years.
27518.m: After the fall of Nineveh the Assyrian Empire fell apart.

27519.e: The Babylonian king Nabopolassar formed an alliance with the Medes from Iran. Together they defeated the Assyrians.
27519.m: Babylonians and Medes conquered Nineveh together.

27520.q: According to the Bible, which prophet was sent to Nineveh?
27520.e: In the Book of Jonah the prophet is meant to call on the people of Nineveh to change their ways. The story is well known because on the way Jonah is swallowed by a great fish.
27520.m: According to the Bible, the prophet Jonah was sent to Nineveh.

27521.q: What were the walls of the royal palaces in Nineveh decorated with?
27521.e: Stone reliefs showed the kings’ military campaigns, hunts and building works. In Sennacherib’s palace alone they were about three kilometres long.
27521.m: The palaces of Nineveh were decorated with stone reliefs.

27522.q: When was Nineveh excavated by researchers?
27522.e: The Briton Austen Henry Layard dug at Nineveh in the 1840s. Many finds went to the British Museum in London.
27522.m: Nineveh was excavated in the 19th century.

27523.q: In which city are the Hanging Gardens said to have stood?
27523.e: Ancient writers report that King Nebuchadnezzar II had the gardens made in Babylon. They have still not been found today.
27523.m: The Hanging Gardens are said to have stood in Babylon.

27524.q: Why do some researchers doubt that the Hanging Gardens in Babylon really existed?
a: No clear traces have been found
The gardens are said to have been made of gold
27524.e: No certain remains of the gardens have been found in Babylon. Herodotus, who described the city in detail, does not mention them either.
27524.m: Whether the Hanging Gardens existed is uncertain.

27525.q: According to tradition, for whom did the king of Babylon build the Hanging Gardens?
a: For his wife, who was homesick for her mountains
For his soldiers after a victory
For the gods of the sea
27525.e: Queen Amytis came from a mountainous land. In flat Babylon she is said to have been homesick. The green terraces were meant to remind her of her home.
27525.m: The gardens are said to have been built for a homesick queen.

27526.q: Which other building, like the Hanging Gardens, is one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World?
27526.e: The Seven Wonders of the Ancient World include the Pyramids of Giza and the Hanging Gardens. The pyramids are the only one still standing.
27526.m: The Hanging Gardens are one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

27527.q: Why are the gardens of Babylon called “hanging”?
a: The plants grew on high terraces and hung down
They were on a cliff above the sea
27527.e: The gardens are said to have been laid out on terraces one above the other. From below it looked as if the plants were hanging over the walls.
27527.m: The Hanging Gardens were on high terraces.

27528.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Babylon, where people search for the gardens?
27528.e: Babylon lies about 90 kilometres south of Baghdad. Since 2019 the ruins have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
27528.m: The ruins of Babylon are in present-day Iraq.

27529.q: From which river would water have had to be lifted for the gardens in Babylon?
27529.e: Babylon lay on the Euphrates. For plants on high terraces, water would have had to be raised with lifting machines.
27529.m: Babylon lay on the River Euphrates.

27530.q: In which region was the Hittite Empire?
27530.e: The Hittite Empire lay in the centre of Anatolia, in present-day Turkey. Later its influence reached as far as Syria.
27530.m: The Hittites lived in Anatolia in present-day Turkey.

27531.q: With which mighty empire on the Nile did the Hittites make a famous peace treaty?
27531.e: After long fighting, the Hittite king and Pharaoh Ramesses II made peace. The treaty is seen as one of the oldest peace treaties that has come down to us.
27531.m: The Hittites made peace with Egypt.

27532.q: Which gate with two stone beasts of prey is a landmark of Hattusa?
27532.e: At the Lion Gate, two lions carved from the stone stand guard. It was an entrance in the wall of the upper city.
27532.m: The Lion Gate is a landmark of the Hittite capital.

27533.q: Where does a copy of the peace treaty between the Hittites and the Egyptians hang?
a: At the UN headquarters in New York
In the Federal Palace in Bern
In the White House in Washington
27533.e: The treaty between King Hattusili III and Pharaoh Ramesses II is seen as one of the oldest peace treaties that has come down to us. That is why a copy of the clay tablet hangs at the United Nations.
27533.m: A copy of the Hittite-Egyptian peace treaty hangs at the UN.

27534.q: Which language family does the language of the Hittites belong to?
27534.e: Hittite is the oldest Indo-European language recorded in writing. It is therefore distantly related to English, German, Latin and Greek.
27534.m: Hittite is the oldest Indo-European language recorded in writing.

27535.q: What did researchers find in large numbers in the Hittite capital?
27535.e: Thousands of clay tablets were found in Hattusa. Since the Hittite language was deciphered in 1915, they can be read and tell us a lot about the Hittites.
27535.m: Clay tablets reveal a lot about the Hittites.

27536.q: Which weapon made the Hittites especially feared?
27536.e: The Hittites used horse-drawn chariots with a crew of three. With them they could attack quickly and with great force.
27536.m: The Hittites were feared for their chariots.

27537.q: Roughly when did the Hittite Empire fall apart?
27537.e: Around 1200 BC several empires in the eastern Mediterranean collapsed. Hattusa too was abandoned at this time.
27537.m: The Hittite Empire fell apart around 1200 BC.

27538.q: Which empire did Nebuchadnezzar II rule?
27538.e: Nebuchadnezzar II was the most important king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire. Under him Babylon reached its greatest splendour.
27538.m: Nebuchadnezzar II was king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire.

27539.q: Roughly when did Nebuchadnezzar II rule?
27539.e: He ruled from 605 to 562 BC, so for over 40 years. That is about 1100 years after Hammurabi.

27540.q: Which city did Nebuchadnezzar II conquer in 587/586 BC, destroying its temple?
27540.e: After an uprising his army besieged the city and destroyed the temple. After that the kingdom lost its independence.
27540.m: Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed the temple in Jerusalem in 587/586 BC.

27541.q: Which army did Nebuchadnezzar defeat as crown prince in 605 BC?
a: The army of the Germanic peoples
27541.e: At the Battle of Carchemish on the Euphrates he beat the pharaoh’s army. After that Babylon was the leading power in the region.
27541.m: Nebuchadnezzar defeated the Egyptians in 605 BC.

27542.q: Which wonder of the world is often linked with Nebuchadnezzar and Babylon?
27542.e: According to a legend, Nebuchadnezzar had the Hanging Gardens made for his wife. Whether they really existed is still disputed today.
27542.m: The Hanging Gardens are seen as Babylon’s wonder of the world.

27543.q: What did Nebuchadnezzar have built in Babylon for the city god Marduk?
27543.e: Marduk was the chief god of Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar had his temple, the Esagila, and the stepped tower next to it splendidly enlarged.
27543.m: Nebuchadnezzar built great temples for Marduk.

27544.q: In which book of the Bible does a prophet interpret Nebuchadnezzar’s dreams?
27544.e: In the Book of Daniel the king dreams, among other things, of a great statue made of different metals. Daniel interprets this dream for him.
27544.m: In the Book of Daniel the prophet interprets Nebuchadnezzar’s dreams.

27545.q: Which opera by Giuseppe Verdi is named after Nebuchadnezzar?
27545.e: “Nabucco” is the short Italian form of Nebuchadnezzar. The Chorus of the Hebrew Slaves from it is especially famous.

27546.q: Which great empire did Cyrus the Great found?
27546.e: Cyrus II is seen as the founder of the first great Persian empire. It later stretched from Egypt to India.
27546.m: Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire.

27547.q: According to tradition, how did Cyrus often treat conquered peoples?
a: He let them keep their religion and customs
He forced everyone to speak Persian
27547.e: Cyrus was seen as a mild ruler. He often let peoples worship their gods and keep their customs.
27547.m: Cyrus let conquered peoples keep their religion.

27548.q: Which king of Lydia, famous for being rich, did Cyrus defeat?
27548.e: Croesus ruled in Sardis in Lydia and was famous for his wealth. That is why people still say “as rich as Croesus” today.
27548.m: Cyrus defeated the rich Lydian king Croesus.

27549.q: Which famous city did Cyrus conquer in 539 BC?
27549.e: Cyrus entered Babylon in 539 BC. After that the whole of Mesopotamia belonged to the Persian Empire.

27550.q: According to the Bible, what did Cyrus allow the Judeans who had been taken to Babylon to do?
a: Build a city on the Nile
27550.e: According to the Book of Ezra, they were allowed to return and rebuild their temple. That is why Cyrus is shown very positively in the Bible.
27550.m: Cyrus allowed the deported Judeans to return home.

27551.q: In which present-day country is the tomb of Cyrus the Great?
27551.e: The simple stone tomb stands in Pasargadae, the first capital of the Persian Empire, in present-day Iran.
27551.m: The tomb of Cyrus is in present-day Iran.

27552.q: How large did the Persian Empire become under Cyrus and his successors?
a: It stretched from Egypt to India
It reached as far as America
27552.e: Cyrus conquered large areas, his successors even more. The Persian Empire was then the largest empire in the world.
27552.m: The Persian Empire stretched from Egypt to India.

27553.q: According to the historian Herodotus, how did Cyrus the Great die?
27553.e: According to Herodotus, Cyrus fell in 530 BC fighting the Massagetae, a people of horsemen in Central Asia.
27553.m: According to Herodotus, Cyrus fell fighting a people of horsemen.

27554.q: How did Darius I govern his huge Persian Empire?
a: He divided it into provinces with governors
He let all the cities vote for themselves
He left it to the priests
27554.e: Darius divided the empire into provinces called satrapies. Each was run by a governor and had to pay taxes to the king.
27554.m: Darius I divided the Persian Empire into provinces.

27555.q: Which empire did King Darius I rule?
27555.e: Darius I ruled the Persian Empire from 522 to 486 BC. It stretched from Egypt to India.
27555.m: Darius I was king of the Persian Empire.

27557.q: What did Darius I introduce to make trade easier in his empire?
27557.e: Darius had a gold coin minted that is called the daric after him. It was valid throughout the empire.
27557.m: Darius I introduced a standard gold coin.

27559.q: What was there at regular intervals along the Persian Royal Road?
27559.e: There were over 100 stations along the road. There, messengers could change horses and ride on quickly.
27559.m: On the Royal Road messengers changed horses at stations.

27560.q: Through which great empire did the Persian Royal Road run?
27560.e: The road linked important cities of the Persian Empire, from present-day Iran to Asia Minor in present-day Turkey.
27560.m: The Royal Road crossed the Persian Empire.

27561.q: Which canal did Darius I have completed in Egypt?
a: A canal from the Nile to the Red Sea
A canal from the Nile to the Euphrates
A canal through the Isthmus of Corinth
A canal to the Dead Sea
27561.e: The canal linked the Nile with the Red Sea and so the Mediterranean with the Indian Ocean. Darius had inscriptions put up to commemorate its construction.
27561.m: Darius I had a canal from the Nile to the Red Sea completed.

27562.q: What did the Persian kings mainly use Persepolis for?
a: As a splendid residence for festivals and receptions
As a harbour for the war fleet
27562.e: The Persian kings had palaces and halls built in Persepolis. There they received envoys and held great festivals.
27562.m: Persepolis was a splendid residence of the Persian kings.

27563.q: Who had Persepolis set on fire in 330 BC?
27563.e: After his victory over the Persians, Alexander captured the city. Afterwards the palaces burnt down, perhaps as revenge for the destruction of Athens by the Persians.
27563.m: Alexander the Great had Persepolis burnt down in 330 BC.

27564.q: In which present-day country are the ruins of Persepolis?
27564.e: Persepolis lies in south-west Iran, north-east of the city of Shiraz. The ruins are among the best-known sights in the country.
27564.m: The ruins of Persepolis are in Iran.

27565.q: What held up the roof of the great audience hall in Persepolis?
27565.e: The roof of the audience hall rested on 72 columns that were about 20 metres high. Some of them still stand today.
27565.m: The audience hall in Persepolis was a huge hall of columns.

27566.q: What do the famous reliefs on the staircases of Persepolis show?
a: Delegations bringing gifts to the king
27566.e: The reliefs show delegations from many peoples of the empire with gifts such as animals, fabrics and vessels. This shows how large the empire was.
27566.m: The staircase reliefs of Persepolis show gift bearers from many peoples.

27567.q: What can still be seen of Persepolis today?
a: Ruins with columns, stairs and reliefs
Just a hole in the ground
27567.e: The palaces burnt down over 2000 years ago. Columns, stairs, gates and many reliefs have survived. The ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
27567.m: The ruins of Persepolis are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

27568.q: What does the Greek name “Persepolis” mean?
27568.e: The Greek word “polis” means city. The Persians themselves called the place Parsa.
27568.m: Persepolis means city of the Persians.

27569.q: Where does the word “Samaritan”, used for people who help others, come from?
a: From the region of Samaria in ancient Israel
27569.e: Samaria was the capital and region of the northern kingdom of Israel. In the Bible a “Good Samaritan” helps an injured man, hence the name for helpers.
27569.m: Samaritans are named after the region of Samaria.

27570.q: What happened to many people of the northern kingdom of Israel after it was conquered?
27570.e: The Assyrians conquered the northern kingdom in 722 BC. Part of the population was taken to other areas of the empire.
27570.m: After the conquest many people from Israel were deported.

27571.q: According to the Bible, after the death of which king did the kingdom split into Israel and Judah?
27571.e: According to the Bible, the northern tribes refused to accept Solomon’s son as king. So around 926 BC a northern kingdom and a southern kingdom came into being.
27571.m: According to the Bible, the kingdom split after Solomon’s death.

27572.q: According to the Bible, how many tribes belonged to the northern kingdom of Israel?
27572.e: According to the Bible, ten of the twelve tribes of Israel formed the northern kingdom. Because they disappeared after the conquest, people speak of the “lost tribes”.
27572.m: According to the Bible, ten tribes belonged to the northern kingdom of Israel.

27573.q: What was the capital of the Kingdom of Judah?
27573.e: Jerusalem was the seat of the kings and of the temple. Judah was the smaller southern kingdom.
27573.m: Jerusalem was the capital of the Kingdom of Judah.

27574.q: What is the period called when many Judeans were taken to Babylon?
27574.e: After the fall of Jerusalem, part of Judah’s upper class lived in Babylonia for decades. This period had a strong influence on the Jewish religion.
27574.m: The deportation of the Judeans to Babylon is called the Babylonian Exile.
